title: Online Safety, Digital Citizenship & Ethics
tagline: Be smart, safe, and kind online!
intro: Hello, young digital explorers! We spend so much time online these days – for studies, fun, and connecting with friends. Just like we learn road safety, it's super important to learn 'online safety' too. This lesson will help you understand how to navigate the digital world responsibly, protect yourself, and become a great digital citizen.
outcomes: By the end of this lesson, you can identify common online risks and scams.
By the end of this lesson, you can apply strategies to protect your personal information and privacy online.
By the end of this lesson, you can practice ethical behaviour and good manners in digital spaces.
By the end of this lesson, you can recognize the importance of digital well-being and balanced screen time.
By the end of this lesson, you can understand how to report cyberbullying or inappropriate content.

lessons.title: Your digital footprint
lessons.why: Your digital footprint is like a permanent tattoo of everything you do online. Understanding it helps you control your online image and protect your future opportunities, from college admissions to job interviews.

studyPlan.task: Watch a short video explaining digital footprint. (e.g., Common Sense Media on YouTube)
studyPlan.read:
A digital footprint is the unique trail of data you leave behind while using the internet. Think of it like walking on a beach; every step leaves a mark. However, unlike sand where water washes tracks away, the internet acts like wet concrete. Once your data is set, it becomes very difficult to remove. This footprint includes everything from the photos you upload on Instagram to the comments you leave on a YouTube video or even the websites you visit. 

For an Indian student, this might mean a comment you made on a gaming forum three years ago or a photo from a school trip tagged by a friend on Facebook. Even if you think you are anonymous, metadata like your IP address or linked email accounts can connect these actions back to your real identity. 

There are two parts to this: the active footprint, which is what you intentionally share, and the passive footprint, which is information collected about you without you knowing, like your browsing history. To manage this, you must first acknowledge that your online life is not separate from your real life. The first step is awareness. Before you click post or search, remind yourself that you are adding a permanent line to your digital biography that could be read by anyone in the world.
checkpoints: Can I explain the difference between an active and a passive digital footprint?
Do I understand why the internet is compared to wet concrete rather than sand?

studyPlan.task: Ask a parent to search your name online. Note what appears.
studyPlan.read:
Searching for yourself is called 'vanity searching,' but it is actually a vital security measure. It allows you to see what the world sees when they look you up. In India, where competition for college admissions and internships is fierce, many recruiters now perform a quick search of a candidate's name to check their character. If the first thing they see is an unprofessional comment or an inappropriate photo, it could hurt your chances before you even walk into the room. 

To do this effectively, use a search engine like Google or Bing. Try searching your full name in quotation marks, like 'Aarav Sharma,' to find exact matches. You should also search for your name combined with your school or city, such as 'Ananya Iyer Delhi.' This helps narrow down results that are specific to you. 

If you find something you do not like, do not panic. Note down which websites host the information. Sometimes it is an old school newsletter, and other times it might be a social media post from a distant relative. By identifying these links now, you gain the power to manage them. This exercise is not about vanity; it is about taking an inventory of your public reputation.
checkpoints: What are the top three results that appear when my name is searched?
Are there any results that I would not want a future college professor to see?

studyPlan.task: Review your social media profiles (if any) from a public perspective. What would a stranger see?
studyPlan.read:
Social media profiles are often the biggest contributors to a student's digital footprint. While these platforms are meant for friends, they are often more public than we realize. A stranger looking at your profile should see a responsible, creative, or kind individual. If they instead see evidence of cyberbullying, offensive language, or risky behavior, your digital citizenship is compromised. 

Imagine you are applying for a scholarship at a top Indian university like IIT or DU. If a selection committee member visits your profile, what vibe do they get? Do you look like someone who contributes positively to their community? To check this, most platforms like Facebook or LinkedIn have a 'View As' feature that lets you see your profile as a member of the public would. 

Pay close attention to your bio, your profile picture, and the 'About' section. Even if your posts are private, your profile picture and cover photo are often public by default. Ensure these images represent you in a way you are proud of. If you see posts that no longer reflect who you are today, consider deleting them or changing their visibility to 'Only Me'. Your profile is your personal brand, so curate it with care.
checkpoints: Does my public profile picture look appropriate for a student?
If a stranger saw my bio today, what three words would they use to describe me?

studyPlan.task: Check your old email IDs. Are there any dormant accounts you should close?
studyPlan.read:
Many of us have 'ghost accounts'—old email IDs created when we were younger for games, forums, or early social media. Often, these accounts have usernames that seemed cool at age ten but look unprofessional at age eighteen. For example, using an email like 'cool_gamer_123@gmail.com' for a formal internship application is a bad idea. Furthermore, these old accounts often have weak passwords and no two-factor authentication, making them easy targets for hackers. 

When a hacker gains access to an old, dormant account, they can find personal information that adds to your digital footprint in a negative way, or they can use it to impersonate you. It is important to consolidate your digital life. Decide on one professional email address, usually a variation of your name, for all official work. 

Go through your old inbox and look at the 'Welcome' emails from services you no longer use. If you find accounts for old forums, shopping sites, or defunct social networks, take the time to log in and deactivate or delete those accounts entirely. This reduces your 'attack surface' and ensures that old, irrelevant data about you is scrubbed from the web. Cleaning up your digital past is just as important as managing your digital present.
checkpoints: How many old accounts do I have that are no longer useful?
Is my primary email address professional enough for a job application?

studyPlan.task: Spend 15 minutes checking privacy settings on one social media app.
studyPlan.read:
Privacy settings are your first line of defense in controlling your digital footprint. Most Indian students use apps like WhatsApp, Instagram, or Snapchat, but few actually read the privacy updates. By default, many apps share more data than necessary, such as your precise location, your 'Last Seen' status, or who can tag you in photos. 

Taking fifteen minutes to audit your settings can significantly change how much of your footprint is visible. For instance, on Instagram, you can set your account to private so only approved followers see your posts. You can also turn off 'Sharing to Stories' to prevent others from easily spreading your content. On WhatsApp, you can restrict your profile photo and 'About' info to 'My Contacts' only. 

Another critical setting is 'Tag Review.' This prevents photos that others take of you from appearing on your profile without your permission. If a friend posts a photo of you at a party that you don't like, having Tag Review enabled ensures it doesn't automatically link to your digital footprint. Remember, technology companies update these settings frequently, so making this a monthly habit is essential for maintaining your digital boundaries.
checkpoints: Is my account set to private, and do I know everyone on my followers list?
Have I enabled 'Tag Review' to control which photos appear on my profile?

studyPlan.task: Write down how you want your digital footprint to look in 5 years.
studyPlan.read:
Your digital footprint doesn't always have to be a list of things you shouldn't do. It can also be a powerful tool to build a positive reputation. As you prepare for your career in India's competitive job market, think about what you want an employer to find when they search for you in five years. Do you want them to find your research papers, your volunteer work with an NGO, or your photography portfolio? 

This is called a 'positive footprint.' Instead of just hiding the bad, you should actively create the good. You can start by sharing articles related to your interests, participating in professional discussions on platforms like LinkedIn, or starting a blog about a hobby you are passionate about. 

Visualize your future self. If you want to be an engineer, your footprint should show your interest in technology and problem-solving. If you want to be an artist, it should showcase your creativity. By being intentional today, you ensure that your digital trail becomes a bridge to your future opportunities rather than a barrier. Start treating your online presence like a digital resume that grows with you.
checkpoints: What are three positive things I want people to find out about me online in the future?
What steps can I take today to start building a professional online presence?

studyPlan.task: Make a small list of one or two things you can do to improve your digital footprint.
studyPlan.read:
Now that you understand what a digital footprint is and how it affects your future, it is time to take action. A cleanup plan is a set of specific tasks to improve your online image. This isn't a one-time event but a lifestyle change in how you interact with technology. 

Start by deleting any posts or comments that you identified earlier in the week as being potentially harmful or embarrassing. If you cannot delete a post because someone else posted it, reach out to them politely and ask them to remove it or untag you. Next, update your passwords and enable two-factor authentication on your most important accounts to prevent identity theft. 

Finally, commit to the 'Pause Rule.' Before posting anything, wait sixty seconds and ask: 'Would I be comfortable if this was printed on the front page of a newspaper?' or 'Would my parents be proud of this?' If the answer is no, don't post it. Managing your digital footprint is about being the boss of your own data. By staying disciplined and checking your presence regularly, you protect your reputation and ensure that your online trail always leads toward success.
checkpoints: What are the two most important changes I made to my online presence this week?
What is the 'Pause Rule,' and how will I use it going forward?

notes: Every click, post, photo, and comment you make online creates your digital footprint.
Your digital footprint is largely permanent and can be seen by colleges, employers, and others.
There are two types: active (what you share) and passive (data collected about you).
Think before you post: 'Would I be okay with my parents or future boss seeing this?'
Regularly review your privacy settings on all online platforms.
Untag yourself from photos you don't want associated with you.
Be careful about sharing personal information like your full address or school name.
A positive digital footprint can open doors for you in academics and career.

caseStudies.title: The College Admissions Scandal
caseStudies.story: In 2017, Harvard University revoked admissions offers to at least ten incoming freshmen after discovering offensive memes and posts they had shared in a private Facebook group. These posts, though in a private group, were eventually brought to the university's attention.
caseStudies.takeaway: Even seemingly private online activities can have serious consequences for your future opportunities.

caseStudies.title: The Delhi Public School Cyberbullying Case
caseStudies.who: Students of a prominent Delhi school
caseStudies.story: In 2020, a private Instagram group chat involving students from a Delhi Public School came to light. The chat contained highly offensive and misogynistic content targeted at female students. The incident led to police complaints, immense public outrage, and disciplinary action against the involved students, severely impacting their reputations and academic standing.
caseStudies.takeaway: Your online actions, even in 'private' groups, can spread widely and cause real harm, affecting your reputation and legal standing.

lessons.practice: Google your own name (and common variations) in incognito mode. See what information is publicly available about you. Then, check your main social media profile and review its privacy settings, ensuring only people you trust can see your posts.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an active and a passive digital footprint?
quiz.a: An active digital footprint is data you intentionally share (posts, comments). A passive digital footprint is data collected about you without your direct input (website cookies, browsing history).

quiz.q: Why is it important to think twice before posting something online?
quiz.a: Because once something is online, it's very difficult to remove completely, and it can be seen by anyone, including future colleges or employers, impacting your reputation.

quiz.q: Name one tool you can use to check your own digital footprint.
quiz.a: Searching your name on Google or other search engines is a good starting point.

lessons.title: Passwords and account security
lessons.why: Strong passwords and smart account security are your first line of defence against online theft and identity fraud. Protecting your accounts means protecting your personal information, money, and digital life.

studyPlan.task: Learn about the characteristics of a strong password (length, mix of characters).
studyPlan.read:
Think of your password as the digital lock to your home. If the lock is flimsy, anyone can walk in. A strong password is your first line of defense. The Gold Standard for a password today is a minimum of 12 characters. While 8 used to be enough, modern hacking tools can crack short passwords in seconds. The key is complexity through a mix of four ingredients: uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and special symbols like @, #, or $. 

For an Indian student, a common mistake is using a simple word like 'Cricket' or 'Bollywood'. Instead, try the 'Sentence Method'. Think of a sentence that is easy for you to remember but hard for others to guess. For example, 'I love eating 2 Samosas every Friday!' could become 'Il2SeF!'. This uses the first letter of each word, maintains the numbers, and adds a special character. It is short to type but incredibly hard for a computer to guess because it does not follow a dictionary pattern.

To build a strong password, avoid dictionary words entirely. Even if you replace 'a' with '@', hackers know these tricks. The best passwords are those that look like random noise to others but have a secret meaning to you. By combining length with variety, you make it mathematically difficult for malicious software to 'brute force' your account. Always remember: length is often more important than complexity, so try to reach that 12 to 15 character mark whenever possible.
checkpoints: What are the four types of characters that should be mixed in a strong password?
Why is a 12-character password safer than an 8-character one?
How does the 'Sentence Method' help in creating a memorable but complex password?

studyPlan.task: Identify common weak passwords and why they are easily guessed.
studyPlan.read:
Many people fall into the trap of convenience when creating passwords. Common mistakes include using personal information that is easily found on social media. For example, a student named Arjun living in Delhi might use 'Arjun@2008' or 'DPSDelhi123'. Because your name, birth year, and school are often public knowledge or easily guessed by classmates, these passwords offer almost no protection. 

Another dangerous habit is using 'Sequential Patterns' or 'Keyboard Walks'. Patterns like '123456', 'qwerty', or 'password' are the first things hackers try. Even slightly more complex patterns like 'asdfgh' are indexed in hacking databases. If you can find the word in a dictionary or see the pattern on your keyboard, it is a weak password. 

Perhaps the biggest mistake is 'Password Reuse'. If you use the same password for your Instagram, your school portal, and your Zomato account, you are creating a single point of failure. If a small food delivery app has a data leak, hackers will take your email and that password and try them on Gmail or Net Banking. This is called 'Credential Stuffing'. To stay safe, ensure every single account has a unique password. If one gets compromised, your other accounts remain safe behind their own unique locks. Never trade security for the convenience of remembering just one word.
checkpoints: Why is it risky to use your birth year or school name in a password?
What is 'Credential Stuffing' and how does it affect users with reused passwords?
Why are keyboard patterns like 'qwerty' considered weak?

studyPlan.task: Explore what a password manager is and how it works (e.g., LastPass, Bitwarden).
studyPlan.read:
If you follow the rule of having a unique, 12-character password for every account, you will quickly find it impossible to remember them all. This is where a Password Manager comes in. Think of it as a highly secure, encrypted digital vault. Instead of memorizing fifty different passwords, you only need to remember one very strong 'Master Password' to unlock the vault. Tools like Bitwarden, LastPass, or Dashlane are reputable options that help manage your digital life.

When you use a password manager, it does two main things: it generates truly random passwords (like 'xK9#vP2!zLq') and it stores them safely. When you visit a website, the manager can automatically fill in your credentials. This prevents you from falling for phishing sites, as the manager will only auto-fill on the legitimate URL it has saved. 

To get started, research a free, reputable password manager. Set it up on your phone or laptop. Create your Master Password—make this one the strongest you have ever made, perhaps a long phrase only you know. Once set up, begin moving your accounts into the manager one by one. You no longer have to worry about forgetting a password or using weak ones because the software handles the complexity for you. It is the most effective way to maintain high security without the mental stress of memorization.
checkpoints: What is the role of a 'Master Password' in a password manager?
How does a password manager help prevent you from falling for phishing websites?
Name two reputable password managers available for students.

studyPlan.task: Understand what 2FA is and why it's crucial for security.
studyPlan.read:
Two-Factor Authentication, or 2FA, is like having a double lock on your door. Even if a thief steals your key (your password), they still cannot get in because they do not have the second key. This second factor is usually something you have, like your smartphone. When you log in, the app asks for your password and then a second verification step, such as a code sent via SMS or a notification on an authenticator app. 

For Indian students, 2FA is commonly seen during online shopping as an 'OTP' (One Time Password). However, you should enable this for all your social media and email accounts, not just for payments. While SMS-based OTPs are common, they can be intercepted. A more secure method is using an 'Authenticator App' like Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator. These apps generate a new 6-digit code every 30 seconds that never leaves your device.

To enable this, go to the 'Security' settings of your favorite app, like WhatsApp or Instagram, and look for 'Two-Factor Authentication'. Follow the steps to link your phone. It might take an extra five seconds to log in, but it makes your account nearly impossible to hack remotely. Even if a hacker across the world gets your password, they will be blocked because they don't have your physical phone to provide the second code.
checkpoints: Why is 2FA described as a 'double lock' for digital accounts?
Which is more secure: an SMS-based OTP or an Authenticator App code?
Where can you usually find the option to turn on 2FA in most apps?

studyPlan.task: Learn how to check if your email has been part of a data breach (e.g., Have I Been Pwned?).
studyPlan.read:
Sometimes, your account security is compromised not because of your mistake, but because a company you use was hacked. This is called a 'Data Breach'. When a company like a social media platform or an e-commerce site is breached, hackers steal databases containing millions of usernames and passwords. They then sell these lists on the dark web. 

You need to know if your information is out there. A famous and safe website for this is 'Have I Been Pwned?'. By entering your email address, the site checks it against thousands of known data breaches. If your email shows up as 'pwned', it tells you exactly which website lost your data and what type of information was leaked. 

If you find your email has been part of a breach, do not panic, but act immediately. First, change the password for that specific service. Second, if you were using that same password for other accounts, change those too. This is why unique passwords are so important—a breach at a small movie ticket site shouldn't put your primary Gmail at risk. Make it a habit to check your email status on these breach-check sites every few months to stay informed about your digital exposure.
checkpoints: What is a data breach and how does it affect your personal security?
What should you do immediately if you discover your email was part of a breach?
Why is the website 'Have I Been Pwned?' useful for digital citizenship?

studyPlan.task: Understand why keeping your software and apps updated is important for security.
studyPlan.read:
Software developers are in a constant race against hackers. When a weakness is found in an app or an operating system, developers release a 'patch' or an 'update' to fix it. If you ignore those 'Update Available' notifications on your phone or laptop, you are leaving your digital windows unlocked. Hackers love users who run outdated software because they can use known exploits to bypass security without even needing a password.

Security updates are not just about new features or emojis; they often include critical fixes for 'Zero-Day vulnerabilities'—flaws that hackers are actively using to infect devices. For an Indian student using a Windows laptop or an Android phone, keeping the OS updated is the most basic form of digital hygiene. 

To stay safe, enable 'Automatic Updates' in your settings. This ensures your device downloads and installs security patches as soon as they are ready. Additionally, keep your web browser (like Chrome or Firefox) updated, as this is your main gateway to the internet. An updated browser can detect malicious websites and block them before they load. Think of updates as an immune system boost for your devices; without them, your hardware is vulnerable to the latest digital viruses and malware.
checkpoints: What is a 'patch' and why do developers release them?
Why is it dangerous to ignore system update notifications?
How does an updated web browser contribute to your online safety?

studyPlan.task: Identify 3-5 accounts you use most and plan to update their passwords and enable 2FA.
studyPlan.read:
Now that you have learned the principles of password strength, managers, 2FA, and updates, it is time to take action. Security is not a one-time event; it is a habit. Today, you will create a 'Security Audit' for your own digital life. Start by identifying your most critical accounts. For most students, these are your primary Email (used for recovery), your main Social Media (Instagram/WhatsApp), and any Educational or Banking portals.

Follow these three steps for each of these top accounts. First, check the password strength. If it is short or contains your name, change it to a 12+ character unique phrase. Second, enable Two-Factor Authentication using an app or SMS. Third, check if your recovery phone number and backup email are correct. Often, we set these up years ago and forget that the old number no longer works. 

By securing these 'anchor' accounts, you protect the rest of your digital identity. If your primary email is secure, it is much harder for a hacker to reset passwords for your other apps. Document which accounts you have secured (but never write down the passwords themselves!). Moving forward, make it a rule that every new account you create gets a unique, manager-generated password from day one. You are now equipped to navigate the digital world with confidence and safety.
checkpoints: Which three accounts are usually considered the most critical to secure first?
Why is it important to verify your recovery phone number and email?
What is the first step you should take if you suspect an account has been compromised?

notes: A strong password should be at least 12 characters long and include a mix of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols.
Avoid using personal information like your name, birthdate, or school name in passwords.
Never use the same password for multiple accounts – if one account is compromised, they all are.
Consider using a reputable password manager to generate and store strong, unique passwords securely.
Enable Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) or Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on all important accounts for an extra layer of security.
Be wary of phishing attempts (fake emails/messages) asking for your password or personal details.
Regularly update your operating system, web browser, and all applications to patch security vulnerabilities.
If you suspect your account is compromised, change your password immediately and review recent activity.

caseStudies.title: The Equifax Data Breach
caseStudies.story: In 2017, Equifax suffered a massive data breach due to a vulnerability in their software, affecting the personal information of 147 million people, including names, birthdates, addresses, and Social Security Numbers. This allowed criminals to potentially open new accounts or commit identity theft.
caseStudies.takeaway: Even large companies can be vulnerable; it highlights the need for individuals to secure their own accounts and data where possible, and for companies to maintain robust security.

caseStudies.title: The Microsoft account hacks
caseStudies.story: Reports often emerge of Microsoft accounts being compromised due to weak passwords, phishing attacks, or recycled passwords from other data breaches. In some instances, hackers gained access to emails, cloud storage (OneDrive), and even financial information linked to the accounts. Microsoft continually urges users to enable 2FA.
caseStudies.takeaway: Using strong, unique passwords and enabling Two-Factor Authentication are critical steps to protect your personal digital accounts from hackers.

lessons.practice: Pick your two most important online accounts (e.g., email and one social media). Change their passwords to something very strong and unique (at least 12 characters, mixed case, numbers, symbols). Then, enable Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) on both if you haven't already. (You might need a parent's help for this step).

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended length for a strong password?
quiz.a: At least 12 characters, ideally more.

quiz.q: Why should you use Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)?
quiz.a: 2FA adds an extra layer of security, requiring a second verification method (like a code from your phone) even if someone has your password, making it much harder for hackers to access your account.

quiz.q: What is a 'phishing' attempt?
quiz.a: A phishing attempt is a deceptive message, usually an email or text, designed to trick you into revealing sensitive information like passwords or bank details by impersonating a trustworthy entity.

lessons.title: Privacy settings and data sharing
lessons.why: Understanding privacy settings and data sharing lets you decide who sees your information and how companies use it. This helps you protect your personal life, prevent unwanted advertising, and maintain control over your digital identity.

studyPlan.task: Watch a video explaining why personal data is valuable and how companies use it.
studyPlan.read:
Data privacy is essentially the right to control how your personal information is collected, used, and shared. In the physical world, you wouldn't give your home address or phone number to a stranger on the street, yet we often share this information digitally without thinking. Your personal data including your name, age, Aadhaar number, location history, and even your shopping preferences is considered the 'new oil.' Companies value this data because it allows them to build a digital profile of you to predict your behavior and target you with specific advertisements.

Imagine a student in Delhi named Rahul who loves cricket. Because he frequently searches for cricket scores and follows players, sports brands will pay to show him ads for expensive shoes. While this might seem harmless, this data can also be used for more intrusive purposes, such as price discrimination or influencing your political views. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 in India now grants you rights to know how your data is being used, but the first line of defense is your own awareness.

To begin protecting yourself, you must first understand that every 'free' app you use is likely paying for its operations by selling access to your data. Start by identifying what information you consider private. A simple method is the 'Public Square Test': if you wouldn't feel comfortable announcing a piece of information in the middle of a crowded market or school assembly, it should probably stay private online.
checkpoints: Why is personal data compared to 'oil' in the digital economy?
What is the name of the recent Indian law that protects your digital data?

studyPlan.task: Review permissions for 2-3 apps on your phone. Do they need access to your camera, microphone, location?
studyPlan.read:
When you install an app on your smartphone, it often asks for 'permissions.' These are requests to access specific hardware or software functions of your device, such as your camera, microphone, contacts, or GPS. While a navigation app like Google Maps legitimately needs your location, a simple flashlight app or a basic calculator app definitely does not. Granting excessive permissions is a major privacy risk because it allows apps to collect data in the background without you noticing.

Consider an Indian student named Priya who downloads a new photo editing app. Upon opening, the app asks for access to her contacts and microphone. Since a photo editor only needs access to the gallery, Priya should be suspicious. Why would the app need to hear her conversations or know who her friends are? This is often a tactic to harvest data for marketing or to build a social graph of the user's network.

To audit your permissions, go to your phone's Settings, then to 'Privacy' or 'Apps.' Look for 'Permission Manager.' Systematically check which apps have access to 'Microphone' and 'Location.' If you see an app that doesn't need a specific permission to function, revoke it immediately. Most modern phones also allow you to select 'Only while using the app,' which is a much safer choice than 'Always allow.'
checkpoints: Give an example of a permission that a calculator app should not require.
Where in your phone settings can you find the Permission Manager?

studyPlan.task: Explore privacy settings on your primary social media platform (e.g., Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook).
studyPlan.read:
Social media platforms like Instagram and Snapchat are designed to be social, but that doesn't mean your profile should be an open book. Default settings are often designed to make your data as public as possible to encourage engagement. However, keeping your profile public means anyone, including scammers or people with bad intentions, can see your photos, your school details, and who your family members are.

For example, an Indian teenager might post a photo in their school uniform. If their account is public, a stranger can easily identify their school, their general age, and their daily routine. By switching to a 'Private Account,' the student ensures that only people they have personally approved can see their content. This creates a safe digital bubble where you can share memories without exposing yourself to the entire internet.

To secure your social media, navigate to the 'Settings and Privacy' menu of your favorite app. First, toggle your account to Private. Second, look for 'Tagging and Mentions' and set it so that you must manually approve any photo you are tagged in. Finally, check the 'Story Sharing' options to prevent strangers from sharing your personal stories to their own profiles. Regularly reviewing these settings is vital because platforms often update their terms and layouts.
checkpoints: What are the benefits of switching from a public account to a private account?
Why should you enable 'Manual Tag Approval' on social media?

studyPlan.task: Learn about browser privacy settings and how to clear cookies and browsing history.
studyPlan.read:
Your web browser is the window through which you view the internet, but it also records everything you do. Cookies are small files stored on your computer by websites to remember your login info or items in a shopping cart. However, 'third-party cookies' are used by advertisers to track you across different websites. If you look at a pair of shoes on one site and then see ads for those same shoes on a news site, that is the work of tracking cookies.

An Indian student researching college applications might notice that after visiting a few university websites, they are suddenly bombarded with ads for coaching centers and student loans. This happens because the browser has saved their search history and shared it with ad networks. Understanding how to manage these digital crumbs is essential for maintaining a clean and private digital footprint.

To take control, go to your browser settings (like Chrome or Edge) and find 'Privacy and Security.' You should regularly use the 'Clear Browsing Data' option to delete cookies and your history. For a more permanent solution, look for 'Block third-party cookies.' Additionally, consider using 'Incognito' or 'Private' mode when searching for sensitive topics, as this prevents the browser from saving your history locally after the session ends.
checkpoints: What is the difference between a first-party cookie and a third-party tracking cookie?
Does 'Incognito' mode make you completely invisible to the websites you visit?

studyPlan.task: Check which apps or services have access to your location data.
studyPlan.read:
Location data is perhaps the most sensitive information your device collects. It doesn't just show where you are right now; it reveals your daily routines, where you live, where you study, and where you hang out with friends. Over time, this data creates a precise map of your life. In India, with the rise of food delivery and ride-sharing apps, we often leave our GPS on constantly, which provides a goldmine of data for companies.

Think about a student who uses a bike-sharing app. The app needs location to find the bike, but does it need to know where the student is two hours after the ride is over? Many apps continue to track location in the background. This can lead to privacy leaks or even physical safety risks if the data is intercepted or sold to unscrupulous third parties. Your location is your physical privacy, and it deserves strict protection.

To manage this, go to your phone's location settings. You will see a list of apps that have recently accessed your GPS. For every app, ensure the setting is 'Allow only while using.' For apps like weather or calculators, turn location off entirely. Also, disable 'Location History' or 'Significant Locations' in your Google or Apple account settings to prevent the device from keeping a permanent log of every place you have ever visited.
checkpoints: Why is background location tracking more dangerous than active location tracking?
Which setting is generally safer for location access: 'Always Allow' or 'While Using the App'?

studyPlan.task: Change passwords for social media accounts to make them stronger.
studyPlan.read:
A strong password is the primary lock on your digital front door. Many students use easy-to-guess passwords like '123456,' their pet's name, or their birth date. Even worse, many use the same password for their email, Instagram, and school portals. If a hacker gets the password for one account, they immediately gain access to everything else. In the age of automated hacking, a simple six-letter password can be cracked in seconds.

A student named Arjun might think his password 'Arjun2005' is safe, but it contains his name and year of birth, which are easily found online. If Arjun's favorite gaming site gets hacked, the hackers will take his email and that password and try them on his Gmail or bank account. This is called 'credential stuffing,' and it is a very common way that people lose control of their digital identities.

To create a strong password, use a 'passphrase'—a string of four or more random words that are easy for you to remember but hard for computers to guess, such as 'BlueMangoRunFast!'. It should be at least 12 characters long and include numbers and symbols. Most importantly, enable Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) on all important accounts. This requires a second code from your phone, so even if a hacker steals your password, they still cannot get into your account.
checkpoints: What are two common mistakes people make when creating passwords?
How does Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) provide an extra layer of security?

studyPlan.task: Write down 2-3 personal rules for sharing information online.
studyPlan.read:
Maintaining digital privacy is not a one-time task; it is a lifestyle and a set of habits. The internet never forgets, and once information is shared, it is almost impossible to claw back completely. Therefore, every student should have a 'Personal Data Policy'—a set of internal rules that guide how they interact with the digital world. This helps you move from being a passive user to an empowered digital citizen who makes intentional choices.

For an Indian student, this might mean deciding never to share their home address or phone number on a public forum, even if a brand offers a 'free gift' in exchange. It might mean refusing to join a new social media trend that requires uploading sensitive data like biometric face scans. By having these rules ready in advance, you won't be tempted by the convenience or peer pressure of the moment. You are protecting your future self from identity theft and reputation damage.

Your policy should be simple. Rule 1: Always read the 'permissions' pop-up before clicking allow. Rule 2: Never post photos of other people without their permission, respecting their privacy as much as your own. Rule 3: Do a 'privacy check-up' on all social media accounts on the first Sunday of every month. By following these steps, you ensure that technology remains a tool for your benefit rather than a surveillance device that tracks your every move.
checkpoints: What is a 'Personal Data Policy' and why is it useful?
Why should you avoid sharing personal info in exchange for 'free' online gifts?

notes: Your personal data (name, age, location, interests, photos) is valuable to companies for advertising and other purposes.
Regularly review and adjust privacy settings on social media, apps, and websites to control who sees your content.
Be cautious about granting apps excessive permissions, such as access to your microphone, camera, or location, if they don't truly need them.
Before clicking 'Accept All Cookies,' understand what data you're allowing websites to collect about your browsing habits.
Think twice before sharing very personal details online, even with friends; privacy settings can change or be misunderstood.
Consider using a VPN (Virtual Private Network) for added privacy, especially on public Wi-Fi.
Learn about data retention policies: how long companies keep your data, even after you delete an account.
In India, data protection laws like the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, aim to give individuals more control over their data.

caseStudies.title: Cambridge Analytica Data Scandal
caseStudies.story: In 2018, it was revealed that Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm, harvested personal data from millions of Facebook profiles without consent. This data was then allegedly used to build psychological profiles of voters and influence political campaigns, leading to widespread public distrust and government investigations.
caseStudies.takeaway: Your data, even indirectly collected, can be used in ways you never intended, highlighting the importance of understanding data sharing and privacy settings.

caseStudies.title: The 'Truecaller' Controversy in India
caseStudies.story: Truecaller, a popular caller ID app, faced scrutiny in India and globally regarding its privacy practices. Concerns arose about how it built its database by uploading users' entire phonebooks without explicit consent from all contacts, potentially exposing millions of private phone numbers. While Truecaller has since updated its policies, it highlighted how third-party apps can share your data.
caseStudies.takeaway: Always review an app's privacy policy and permissions before installing, especially apps that ask for access to your contacts or other sensitive data.

lessons.practice: Go to the privacy settings of your most used social media app (e.g., Instagram, Snapchat) and spend 15-20 minutes carefully reviewing each option. Adjust them to your comfort level, ensuring you understand who can see your posts, stories, and personal information.

quiz.q: Why is it important to review app permissions regularly?
quiz.a: Reviewing app permissions ensures that apps only have access to the data they genuinely need, preventing unnecessary sharing of your location, contacts, or other sensitive information.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of privacy settings on social media?
quiz.a: Privacy settings on social media allow you to control who can see your posts, profile information, and interact with you, thus managing your online visibility and safety.

quiz.q: What is one way companies use your personal data?
quiz.a: Companies often use your personal data to tailor advertisements to your interests, improve their services, or for market research.

lessons.title: Spotting misinformation and deepfakes
lessons.why: In today's digital world, misinformation and deepfakes can mislead you, influence your opinions, and even cause harm. Learning to spot them helps you make informed decisions and think critically, rather than being fooled by fake news or images.

studyPlan.task: Learn definitions of misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation with examples.
studyPlan.read:
Information travels faster than light in our digital era, but not all of it is true. To be a smart digital citizen, you must first understand the three main categories of false data: misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation. Misinformation is when someone shares false information but doesn't realize it is wrong. For example, your uncle might share a WhatsApp forward about a 'home remedy' for a virus thinking he is helping, even though the remedy is scientifically unproven. The intent is not to harm, but the information is still incorrect.

Disinformation is much more dangerous because it is intentionally created to deceive people. This often happens during elections or to create social unrest. An example would be someone creating a fake news report about a celebrity's death to drive traffic to a website or to cause panic. Malinformation is based on reality but used to inflict harm. This includes leaking someone's private photos or messages out of context to ruin their reputation. While the data might be 'real,' the intent is malicious.

To identify these, you must always look at the intent. Ask yourself: Is the sender trying to help, or are they trying to make me angry, scared, or suspicious? A simple method to handle this is the 'Pause and Reflect' method. Before you react emotionally to a piece of news, take thirty seconds to wonder why this specific information was created and shared with you. Understanding the 'why' behind the message is your first line of defense against being misled.
checkpoints: Can you explain the difference between misinformation and disinformation?
What is an example of malinformation in a social media context?
Why is intent important when evaluating information?

studyPlan.task: Identify common types of misleading content (clickbait, satire, manipulated content).
studyPlan.read:
Fake news isn't just one thing; it comes in many flavors designed to trick your brain. The most common type is clickbait. These are headlines like 'You won't believe what this Indian cricketer said!' which use sensationalism to get you to click a link. The actual story is usually boring or irrelevant. Another type is satire, like websites that write funny, fake stories to poke fun at society. While satire is for entertainment, it becomes fake news when people mistake it for real reporting.

Manipulated content is another major issue. This is when real photos or videos are edited to change their meaning. For example, a video of a political protest might be slowed down to make a speaker look intoxicated, or a photo of a crowded market might be labeled as a recent event when it actually happened five years ago. This is known as 'false context.' Even if the photo is real, the caption makes it a lie.

To spot these, look for emotional triggers. If a headline makes you feel extremely angry or shocked, it is likely designed to be clickbait or manipulated content. A useful step is to read beyond the headline. Often, the first paragraph of a sensational article will reveal that the headline was an exaggeration. Always check if the content is labeled as 'humor' or 'opinion' before taking it as a hard fact. By identifying these formats, you become less susceptible to the emotional manipulation that drives viral fake news.
checkpoints: What is the primary goal of clickbait headlines?
How can a real photo become 'false context' misinformation?
Why should you be wary of articles that trigger strong emotions?

studyPlan.task: Explore reputable fact-checking websites (e.g., Alt News, Boom Live, Snopes).
studyPlan.read:
You don't have to be an expert to verify the news; you just need to know where the experts are. Fact-checking organizations are professional groups that investigate viral claims. In India, platforms like Alt News and Boom Live are dedicated to debunking viral myths, especially those circulating on WhatsApp and Twitter. These organizations use forensic tools to trace the origin of photos and videos to see if they have been edited or misused.

International sites like Snopes or the Reuters Fact Check department are also excellent for global news. These sites provide detailed reports explaining exactly why a claim is false, showing the original sources and evidence. If you see a suspicious claim about a new government scheme or a viral health tip, your first step should be to visit one of these sites and type keywords into their search bar. If the story has gone viral, chances are they have already debunked it.

A simple method to follow is the 'Search and Verify' technique. When you receive a doubtful forward, copy a unique sentence from the message and paste it into a search engine followed by the word 'fact check.' If reputable organizations have flagged it, you will see their reports immediately. Using these tools helps you become a source of truth in your friend circles, allowing you to stop the chain of lies before they spread further. Remember, if a story sounds too wild to be true, it probably is.
checkpoints: Name two reputable fact-checking organizations based in India.
How can you use a search engine to verify a viral WhatsApp forward?
Why is it helpful to read a full fact-check report instead of just the verdict?

studyPlan.task: Practice evaluating news sources using criteria like author, date, and bias.
studyPlan.read:
Not all sources of information are equal. Evaluating source reliability is a core skill for any digital citizen. When you encounter an article, first look at the 'About Us' section of the website. A reliable news organization will have a physical address, a clear list of editors, and a history of professional reporting. Be wary of websites that have strange URLs, such as those ending in '.com.co' or other odd extensions meant to mimic real news sites.

Next, check the author's credentials. Is the person a journalist with a track record, or is the post anonymous? Look at the date of publication as well. Sometimes, old news from years ago is reshared as if it happened today to create panic. Bias is another factor; every source has a perspective, but a reliable source sticks to facts and presents multiple sides of a story rather than just using loaded, insulting language.

Practice the 'IMVAIN' method to evaluate sources: Is the source Independent? Multiple sources saying the same thing? Does the source Verify with evidence? Is the source Authoritative or Informed? Is the source Named? If an article fails most of these checks, it is not a reliable source. For example, if you see a health claim on a random blog without any doctor's name or link to a medical study, you should treat it as false until proven otherwise. Developing this skepticism is vital for your academic and personal life.
checkpoints: What are three red flags in a website's URL or 'About' section?
Why is checking the publication date important for news verification?
What does it mean for a source to be 'Independent' and 'Informed'?

studyPlan.task: Watch a video demonstrating what a deepfake is and how it works.
studyPlan.read:
Deepfakes represent the next frontier of digital deception. The word is a combination of 'deep learning' and 'fake.' These are videos, audio recordings, or images created using Artificial Intelligence that look and sound like real people. AI models are trained on thousands of photos and voice samples of a person until they can generate new footage of that person saying or doing things they never actually did. This is much more advanced than simple Photoshop.

For a student in India, this could manifest as a fake video of a principal announcing a school holiday, or more seriously, a fake video of a politician making a controversial statement. While some deepfakes are used for fun, like putting your face into a movie scene via an app, they can be used for 'face swapping' in malicious ways to bully or blackmail individuals. Because they look so realistic, our brains are naturally wired to believe what we see and hear.

Understanding how they work is the first step. AI analyzes the movements of a real person's face and maps them onto the target's face. To stay safe, you must realize that video evidence is no longer the 'absolute truth.' A simple method to stay aware is to always ask: 'Would this person realistically say this?' If a video shows a shy classmate suddenly giving a professional-level hip-hop performance, your first thought should be to check if it's an AI-generated deepfake.
checkpoints: What two technologies or concepts combine to create the term 'Deepfake'?
How does AI create a deepfake video?
Why can deepfakes be more dangerous than traditional photo editing?

studyPlan.task: Learn visual and audio cues that can indicate a deepfake (e.g., unnatural blinking, strange voice).
studyPlan.read:
While AI is getting better at creating deepfakes, it still leaves 'digital fingerprints' that you can spot if you look closely. The most common visual cue is unnatural blinking. Humans blink regularly; AI often struggles to replicate this, so a deepfake character might not blink at all or might blink in a rhythmic, robotic way. Look closely at the edges of the face—where the hair meets the forehead or where the chin meets the neck. In deepfakes, these areas often look blurry or have a strange shimmering effect.

Lighting and shadows are also difficult for AI to get right. If the light on the person's nose doesn't match the light on their cheeks, or if the shadows don't move when they move, it's a sign of manipulation. Audio is another giveaway. Listen for robotic tones, unnatural pauses between words, or a lack of breathing sounds. Sometimes the mouth movements won't perfectly sync with the sounds, similar to a badly dubbed movie.

To practice this, use the 'Zoom and Listen' method. Zoom in on the eyes and mouth of a suspicious video. Look for 'glitches' or pixelation when the person turns their head. Listen to the audio through headphones to catch metallic or distorted sounds. These inconsistencies are the cracks in the AI's mask. As you train your eyes and ears to find these flaws, you will become much harder to deceive.
checkpoints: What is a common sign of a deepfake related to eye movement?
Where should you look on a person's face to find blurring or 'shimmering'?
How can audio quality help you identify a fake video?

studyPlan.task: Develop a personal checklist for evaluating news and media before sharing.
studyPlan.read:
The final step in becoming a responsible digital citizen is moving from a passive consumer to a critical thinker. Every time you are about to hit 'share' or 'like' on a post, you are acting as a publisher. If you share misinformation, you become part of the problem. Critical consumption means treating your social media feed like a courtroom where every post is 'innocent' of being true until it provides enough evidence to be 'guilty' of being a fact.

You should develop a personal verification checklist. Before sharing, ask yourself: 1. Who created this and what is their motive? 2. Is the date current? 3. Can I find this on a reputable news site like The Hindu or NDTV? 4. Does the image look edited or the video look like a deepfake? 5. Why am I sharing this—is it because it's true, or just because I like what it says? This last question is about 'confirmation bias,' where we are more likely to believe things that agree with our existing opinions.

Practice the 'Stop the Spread' rule: If you can't verify it in two minutes using a search engine or a fact-checking site, do not share it. It is better to be silent than to spread a lie. By holding yourself to a high standard of digital ethics, you protect your reputation and contribute to a safer, more truthful internet for everyone in India. Your critical thinking is the most powerful tool you have.
checkpoints: What is 'confirmation bias' and how does it affect our judgment?
What are the five questions on the personal verification checklist?
What is the 'Stop the Spread' rule for social media sharing?

notes: Misinformation is false or inaccurate information, often shared without intent to harm; disinformation is intentionally misleading.
Deepfakes are highly realistic forged videos or audio created using AI, making it seem like someone said or did something they didn't.
Always check the source of information: Is it a reputable news organization, or an unknown social media account?
Look for multiple reliable sources confirming the same story before believing it.
Be suspicious of headlines that are highly emotional, sensational, or seem too good/bad to be true.
Reverse image search can help verify if a picture is old, out of context, or digitally altered.
For deepfakes, look for inconsistencies: unnatural facial movements, strange lighting, pixelation, or unusual voice tones.
Think critically: 'Who created this? Why? What evidence supports it?' before sharing anything online.

caseStudies.title: COVID-19 Misinformation 'Infodemic'
caseStudies.story: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the World Health Organization (WHO) identified an 'infodemic' of misinformation spreading rapidly, leading to false cures, conspiracy theories, and public distrust in health authorities. This led to serious public health consequences, including vaccine hesitancy and adherence to dangerous unproven remedies.
caseStudies.takeaway: Misinformation, especially during crises, can have real-world, dangerous impacts on public health and safety, making critical evaluation essential.

caseStudies.title: Deepfake of a Bollywood Actor
caseStudies.story: In 2023, a deepfake video of popular South Indian actress Rashmika Mandanna went viral, showing her in compromising clothing. The video, expertly manipulated using AI, caused significant distress to the actress and highlighted the growing threat of non-consensual deepfake pornography and identity abuse in India.
caseStudies.takeaway: Deepfakes can be used to harm reputations, spread false narratives, and even facilitate harassment, requiring careful scrutiny of all digital media.

lessons.practice: Find a news article or social media post that seems unusual or highly emotional. Use a fact-checking website (like Alt News or Boom Live for India, or Snopes globally) to verify its claims. If there's an image or video, try a reverse image/video search (e.g., Google Images, TinEye) to check its origin and authenticity.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between misinformation and disinformation?
quiz.a: Misinformation is false information spread unintentionally, while disinformation is false information deliberately created and spread to deceive or cause harm.

quiz.q: Name two visual cues that might indicate a video is a deepfake.
quiz.a: Unnatural or robotic facial expressions, lack of blinking, inconsistent lighting, or strange distortions around the edges of the face are common cues.

quiz.q: What is the first step you should take when you see a suspicious news headline?
quiz.a: The first step is to check the source of the information and look for independent verification from multiple reputable news outlets.

lessons.title: Cyberbullying: prevention and response
lessons.why: Cyberbullying can hurt deeply and affect your confidence and well-being. Knowing how to prevent it and respond safely empowers you to protect yourself and others, ensuring a positive and respectful online environment for everyone.

studyPlan.task: Understand what cyberbullying is and its different forms (harassment, exclusion, impersonation).
studyPlan.read:
Cyberbullying is any form of harassment that happens through digital devices like smartphones, laptops, or tablets. Unlike physical bullying, it can happen 24/7 and reach a wide audience instantly. It is important to recognize that cyberbullying is not just a joke; it is a pattern of behavior intended to shame, anger, or scare those who are targeted.

There are several forms this can take. Harassment involves sending repetitive mean or insulting messages. Exclusion happens when a group deliberately leaves someone out of online chats or gaming groups to make them feel isolated. Impersonation is particularly dangerous, where someone creates a fake profile using your name and photo to post offensive content or ruin your reputation. Another common form is outing, where someone shares your private information or embarrassing photos without your consent.

Imagine a student named Rohan who is part of his school's cricket WhatsApp group. Suddenly, a few classmates start posting edited, insulting photos of him every time he misses a catch. They then create a new group titled 'Rohan is a Loser' and invite everyone except him. This is a clear case of both harassment and exclusion.

To identify cyberbullying, ask yourself three questions: Is this behavior repetitive? Is it intended to cause harm or embarrassment? Is there a power imbalance? If the answer is yes, it is likely cyberbullying.
checkpoints: What are the three main forms of cyberbullying?
How does impersonation differ from simple harassment?
Why is exclusion considered a form of bullying?

studyPlan.task: Learn about the emotional and psychological effects of cyberbullying on victims.
studyPlan.read:
The impact of cyberbullying goes far beyond the screen. Because digital messages are persistent and often public, the emotional damage can feel permanent. For an Indian student, the fear of 'Log Kya Kahenge' (what will people say) adds an extra layer of stress, especially if the bullying involves family or school reputation.

Victims often experience deep emotional distress, including anxiety, sadness, and a loss of confidence. Physically, the stress can manifest as headaches, stomach aches, or an inability to sleep. Academically, students who are cyberbullied often find it hard to concentrate on their studies, leading to a sudden drop in grades or a desire to skip school entirely to avoid facing their peers.

Consider Priya, a bright student who loves posting her poetry on Instagram. After a group of strangers and schoolmates start leaving hateful comments about her appearance and intelligence, she begins to feel ashamed. She stops writing, deletes her account, and starts avoiding her friends in the canteen. She feels like everyone is judging her, even those who haven't seen the comments.

It is crucial to understand that these feelings are a normal reaction to an abnormal situation. Cyberbullying affects the brain's stress response. Recognizing these signs early—such as feeling nervous when a notification pops up or withdrawing from social activities—is the first step toward seeking help and healing.
checkpoints: What are two physical symptoms of cyberbullying stress?
How can cyberbullying affect a student's academic life?
Why does the public nature of the internet make the impact worse?

studyPlan.task: Discuss how to maintain online privacy and think before posting to avoid being a target.
studyPlan.read:
Prevention is about building a digital shield around your personal life. While you cannot control what others do, you can control how much access they have to you. Maintaining online privacy is the most effective way to minimize the risk of becoming a target. This involves more than just setting a strong password; it involves curating your digital footprint.

A simple rule for Indian students is to 'Think Before You Post'. Before sharing a photo, a location tag, or a personal opinion, ask yourself if you would be comfortable with your principal or your parents seeing it. Once something is online, you lose control over how it is shared or edited. Avoid sharing private details like your home address, school name, or phone number on public platforms.

For example, if Arjun is excited about his new bike and posts a photo with his house number clearly visible in the background, he is unintentionally giving away his location to strangers. A better approach is to crop the photo to show only the bike and set his profile to 'Private' so only trusted friends can see it.

Steps for prevention: First, go to your privacy settings on apps like Instagram and WhatsApp and restrict who can see your status and photos. Second, never share your passwords with friends, even best friends. Third, be selective about whom you accept as a friend or follower. If you don't know them in real life, don't let them into your digital life.
checkpoints: What does 'Think Before You Post' mean in practice?
Why should you keep your social media profiles private?
Name one piece of personal information you should never share online.

studyPlan.task: Learn the 'Stop, Block, Tell' approach (don't respond, block the bully, tell a trusted adult).
studyPlan.read:
If you find yourself being targeted by a cyberbully, the most important thing to remember is that it is not your fault. The natural instinct might be to argue back or defend yourself, but this is exactly what the bully wants. They seek a reaction. Instead, follow the 'Stop, Block, Tell' method.

Stop: Do not respond to mean messages. Responding often escalates the situation and gives the bully more material to use against you. Take a deep breath and put the phone away. Block: Use the block feature immediately on all platforms where the bullying is happening. This cuts off the bully's access to you and prevents further harassment. Tell: Reach out to a trusted adult. This could be a parent, a favorite teacher, or a school counselor. Sharing the burden makes it manageable.

Crucially, you must save evidence before blocking. Take screenshots of messages, comments, or posts. In India, under the IT Act, digital evidence is necessary if you need to file a formal complaint. Do not delete the messages until they are recorded.

For instance, if Anjali receives threatening DMs on Snapchat, she should take screenshots, block the user immediately, and show the screenshots to her mother or a teacher. By not replying, Anjali denies the bully the satisfaction of a reaction and keeps a record of the incident for safety.
checkpoints: Why is it a bad idea to respond to a cyberbully?
What is the first thing you should do after receiving a mean message?
Why are screenshots important when reporting bullying?

studyPlan.task: Understand your role as a bystander and how to support a friend who is being cyberbullied.
studyPlan.read:
Most cyberbullying happens in front of an audience. These are the bystanders—people who see the bullying but don't say anything. Often, bystanders stay silent because they are afraid of becoming the next target. However, staying silent can be seen as supporting the bully. You have the power to change the situation by becoming an 'Upstander'.

Being an upstander doesn't mean you have to start a fight with the bully. In fact, arguing online can be counterproductive. Instead, support the victim privately. Send them a message saying, 'I saw what happened, and it wasn't right. Are you okay?' This simple act can greatly reduce the victim's feeling of isolation. 

You can also take action without direct confrontation by reporting the offensive post or comment anonymously. If the bullying is happening in a group chat, you can steer the conversation in a different direction or state firmly that the behavior is not cool. 

Imagine Kabir sees his friend Meera being mocked in a tuition class group chat. Instead of laughing along or staying quiet, Kabir sends Meera a private message to check on her and then tells their teacher about the group's behavior. By doing this, Kabir shows Meera she isn't alone and ensures the teacher can intervene. Upstanders create a culture where bullying is not tolerated, making the digital space safer for everyone.
checkpoints: What is the difference between a bystander and an upstander?
How can you support a friend who is being bullied without arguing with the bully?
Why is private messaging a victim helpful?

studyPlan.task: Learn how to use reporting features on social media platforms and school reporting systems.
studyPlan.read:
Every major social media platform has built-in tools to handle abuse. Knowing how to use these tools is a vital digital skill. Reporting is not 'tattling'; it is a way to hold users accountable for violating community standards. Most platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and X (Twitter) keep reports anonymous, so the bully won't know who reported them.

To report content, look for the three dots (...) or the 'Options' menu near the comment or post. Select 'Report' and follow the prompts to categorize the abuse (e.g., harassment, hate speech, or sharing private images). For serious cases involving threats of violence or explicit content, you can also report to the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal of India (cybercrime.gov.in). 

Schools in India are also increasingly adopting anti-bullying policies. If the bullying involves schoolmates, your school’s grievance cell or counselor is an official channel for help. They can mediate the situation and ensure the bully faces consequences within the school system.

Suppose Sameer sees a fake profile created in his friend's name. He should first report the profile to the platform as 'Impersonation'. Then, he should help his friend gather the URL of the fake profile and report it to the school authorities or the local cyber cell if the profile is posting harmful content. Using these formal channels ensures that the platform's moderators take action to remove the content.
checkpoints: Where can you find the report button on most social media apps?
What is the official Indian government website for reporting cybercrimes?
Is reporting anonymous on social media platforms?

studyPlan.task: Commit to one act of kindness or positive interaction online this week.
studyPlan.read:
The final step in combating cyberbullying is to actively build a positive online culture. Digital citizenship is not just about avoiding bad behavior; it is about using the internet to spread kindness and support. Because text lacks tone and facial expressions, it is easy for messages to be misunderstood. Being intentionally kind helps prevent these misunderstandings.

Online kindness can be simple. It could be leaving a genuine compliment on a friend's art project, sharing an inspiring story, or thanking someone who helped you with homework in a group chat. These small actions create a 'ripple effect'. When people see others being kind, they are more likely to behave positively themselves.

For your final task, commit to one act of 'Digital Kindness'. Identify someone in your network who might be going through a tough time or someone who recently shared something brave. Send them a supportive comment or a message of appreciation. 

For example, if you see a classmate post a video of themselves practicing a new language or a dance, leave a comment like, 'This is so brave of you to share, keep going!' By choosing to be positive, you are setting a standard for your peers. Remember, the internet is a tool for connection. When we use it with empathy and respect, we make it a place where everyone feels safe to express themselves. You have the power to make the digital world a better place, one message at a time.
checkpoints: What is the 'ripple effect' of online kindness?
Why is it easy for text messages to be misunderstood?
How does positive interaction help prevent cyberbullying?

notes: Cyberbullying is bullying that takes place over digital devices like cell phones, computers, and tablets.
It can include sending mean messages, spreading rumors, sharing embarrassing photos, or excluding someone online.
Never respond to cyberbullying; engaging often makes the situation worse.
Block the cyberbully immediately on all platforms to prevent further contact.
Save evidence (screenshots, messages) of cyberbullying; this is crucial for reporting.
Always tell a trusted adult – a parent, teacher, counsellor – if you or a friend are being cyberbullied.
Use the reporting tools available on social media platforms to report abusive content or users.
Be an Upstander, not a Bystander: Speak up or get help if you see someone else being cyberbullied.

caseStudies.title: Megan Meier Cyberbullying Case
caseStudies.story: In 2006, 13-year-old Megan Meier took her own life after being cyberbullied on MySpace by a fake online persona created by an adult neighbor and her daughter. The case brought widespread attention to the devastating consequences of online harassment and led to legal actions and awareness campaigns.
caseStudies.takeaway: Cyberbullying has severe emotional consequences, and adults can also be perpetrators; it's crucial to report any form of online harassment immediately.

caseStudies.title: Suicide due to Blackmailing in Chennai
caseStudies.story: In 2020, a medical student in Chennai died by suicide after allegedly being cyberbullied and blackmailed by unknown individuals who threatened to publish manipulated images and personal information online if she didn't pay money. This tragic incident highlighted the rise of online extortion and its severe impact, especially on young individuals in India.
caseStudies.takeaway: Cyberbullying can involve blackmail and financial extortion, making it vital to never share personal or compromising information online and to seek help immediately if threatened.

lessons.practice: Identify the 'Report' or 'Block' feature on your two most used social media apps. quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do if you are being cyberbullied?

quiz.q: Why is it important to save evidence of cyberbullying?
