lessons.title: Online scams targeting students
lessons.why: In our digital world, knowing about online scams is like having a superpower to protect your money and personal information. Learning to spot these tricks keeps you safe from fraudsters trying to take advantage of young people.

studyPlan.task: Read about common online scams affecting students (e.g., job scams, scholarship scams).
studyPlan.read:
Welcome to your first day. Online scams are deceptive traps designed to steal your money or identity. For students in India, two common types are job scams and scholarship scams. Fraudsters know that young people are often looking for part-time income or financial aid for college. They use these desires to lure you into sharing sensitive information.

Imagine you receive a WhatsApp message from a recruiter claiming to be from a major Indian tech company. They offer a work-from-home job paying five thousand rupees a day for simple tasks like liking YouTube videos. However, they ask you to pay a small registration fee or a security deposit to get started. This is a classic red flag. Real employers will never ask you for money to give you a job.

Scholarship scams work similarly. You might get an email saying you have been selected for a government grant, but you need to pay a processing fee to claim it. These scams often use official-looking logos of the Ministry of Education to appear legitimate. To protect yourself, always research the organization independently. Never pay money to receive a prize or a job. If someone creates a sense of extreme urgency, take a deep breath and pause. Verify the source by visiting the official website directly instead of clicking links in the message.
checkpoints: What is the main sign of a fake job offer on WhatsApp?
Why would a scammer use a government logo in an email?
What should you do if an offer requires a 'registration fee'?

studyPlan.task: Watch a video on how to identify phishing emails and messages, look for red flags.
studyPlan.read:
Phishing is the digital equivalent of fishing, where scammers use bait to catch you. They send emails or SMS messages that look like they come from your bank, school, or a popular shopping site like Amazon or Flipkart. The goal is to trick you into clicking a link that leads to a fake login page where they can steal your credentials.

Let's look at an example. You get a message saying your bank account will be blocked unless you update your KYC details immediately. The message contains a link. If you look closely at the sender's address, it might be 'support@bank-verify-kYC.com' instead of the official bank domain. The tone is always urgent to make you act without thinking. They want you to panic so you don't notice the small errors.

A simple method to stay safe is the 'Hover and Inspect' rule. If you are on a computer, hover your mouse over the link without clicking. The real destination URL will appear at the bottom of your screen. If the URL looks strange or doesn't match the company name perfectly, it is a scam. On a phone, never click links in SMS regarding bank issues. Instead, open your banking app manually or go to the official website through your browser to check for alerts.
checkpoints: How can you check a link's true destination without clicking it?
What is a common emotional tactic used in phishing messages?
Why should you check the sender's email address carefully?

studyPlan.task: Research how fraudsters use UPI for scams, like 'request money' tricks instead of 'send money'.
studyPlan.read:
In India, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has changed how we handle money, but it has also opened doors for fraudsters. One of the most common tricks is the 'Request Money' scam. Scammers often pose as buyers on platforms like OLX. They tell you they want to buy your item and will send you a QR code to 'receive' the payment.

Here is the vital rule: You never need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money. If a screen asks for your PIN, it means money is being deducted from your account, not added to it. Fraudsters will send a 'Collect Request' on apps like Google Pay or PhonePe. They might say, 'Just tap this and enter your PIN to get the 500 rupees.' The moment you enter that PIN, the money leaves your account and goes to theirs.

To stay safe, always read the screen carefully before tapping. If the button says 'Pay' or 'Send,' you are losing money. Also, be wary of people who insist on using QR codes for payments they owe you. Legitimate transactions where you are the receiver only require your UPI ID or phone number; they do not require you to scan anything or enter a secret code. If someone is rushing you during a payment process, stop the transaction immediately.
checkpoints: Do you ever need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money?
What does a 'Collect Request' on a UPI app actually do?
What should you do if a buyer on OLX sends you a QR code to scan?

studyPlan.task: Identify examples of fake giveaways or 'too good to be true' offers on platforms you use.
studyPlan.read:
Social media platforms like Instagram and Telegram are hotspots for 'too good to be true' offers. You might see an ad for a high-end smartphone at a 90% discount or a giveaway for a free laptop just for filling out a survey. These are almost always scams designed to collect your personal data or install malware on your device.

A common Indian student example involves 'investment' groups on Telegram. You might be added to a group where people post screenshots of making thousands of rupees by investing small amounts in crypto or stocks. The admin will ask you to transfer a small amount to 'double your money.' Once you send the money, they will either ask for more fees or block you entirely. These screenshots are usually fake or manipulated.

To identify these scams, check the profile's authenticity. Does the brand account have a blue tick? Are the comments turned off? If a deal seems impossible, it is. Avoid sharing viral 'giveaway' posts that ask for your phone number or address. Remember, your personal data is valuable. By giving it away to unknown entities, you risk identity theft or being targeted for more sophisticated financial crimes in the future.
checkpoints: What are the signs of a fake giveaway on Instagram?
Why do scammers show fake profit screenshots on Telegram?
What is the risk of sharing your phone number in an online survey?

studyPlan.task: Review tips for creating unique and strong passwords and consider using a password manager.
studyPlan.read:
Your password is the primary key to your digital life. Many students use easy-to-guess passwords like their name followed by '123' or their birth date. This makes it incredibly easy for hackers to use 'brute force' attacks to break into your accounts. Once one account is compromised, they often try the same password on your email and banking apps.

A strong password should be a 'passphrase' rather than a single word. Combine three random words and add numbers and symbols, such as 'BlueLaptop#2024!'. It should be at least 12 characters long. Crucially, you must use a different password for every single service. If you find it hard to remember them, use a reputable password manager. These apps store your passwords securely and can generate complex ones for you.

Additionally, always enable Two-Factor Authentication (2FA). This adds a second layer of security. Even if a scammer steals your password, they cannot log in without the OTP sent to your phone or an authenticator app. Think of your password as the lock on your front door and 2FA as the security guard. Using both makes you a very difficult target for hackers. Check your main accounts today and see which ones are missing this vital extra layer of protection.
checkpoints: What are the three components of a strong passphrase?
Why is it dangerous to use the same password for all accounts?
How does Two-Factor Authentication protect you even if your password is stolen?

studyPlan.task: Learn how to report an online scam to CyberDost or your bank.
studyPlan.read:
If you or someone you know falls victim to a scam, knowing how to react is crucial. The first hour after a scam occurs is called the 'Golden Hour.' If you report a financial fraud within this time, there is a much higher chance that the bank can freeze the transaction and recover your money. Do not let embarrassment stop you from seeking help; scammers are professionals at deception.

In India, the primary resource is the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. You can visit 'cybercrime.gov.in' to file a complaint. You can also call the national helpline number 1930. This is a dedicated line for reporting financial cybercrimes. When you report, keep all evidence ready, including screenshots of the chat, the transaction ID from your payment app, and the phone number or email address of the scammer.

If the scam happened through a bank account, call your bank's official customer care immediately to block your cards and UPI access. You can find these numbers on the back of your debit card or the bank's official website. Reporting doesn't just help you; it helps the authorities track down these criminals and prevents others from being cheated. By documenting the incident, you provide the police with the digital trail needed to investigate the fraud.
checkpoints: What is the Indian national helpline number for cybercrime?
What information should you keep as evidence after a scam?
Why is it important to report a scam within the 'Golden Hour'?

studyPlan.task: Review your social media privacy settings and update any weak passwords.
studyPlan.read:
On this final day, it is time to turn your knowledge into action with a security audit. Start by reviewing your privacy settings on apps like Instagram, WhatsApp, and Facebook. Often, these apps default to sharing your profile picture and 'Last Seen' status with everyone. Change these settings to 'My Contacts' to prevent strangers from gathering information about you to use in a scam.

Next, look at your app permissions. Does a simple calculator app really need access to your contacts or location? If not, revoke those permissions. This limits the amount of data that could be leaked if the app is compromised. Also, check your 'Logged-in Devices' list in your Google or Social Media settings. If you see a device you don't recognize, log it out immediately and change your password.

Finally, talk to your parents or younger siblings. Explain the UPI 'Request Money' trick to them, as older family members are often the biggest targets for these scams. Education is the best defense. By securing your accounts and spreading awareness, you are creating a safer digital environment for yourself and your community. Stay curious, stay skeptical of strange messages, and always prioritize your digital safety over a quick deal or an urgent request.
checkpoints: Which privacy setting on WhatsApp helps prevent strangers from scouting your profile?
Why should you check the 'Logged-in Devices' section of your accounts?
What is one simple way to help your family stay safe from UPI scams?

notes: Be wary of unsolicited messages or calls asking for personal details like OTPs or bank account numbers.
Always verify the sender of an email or message, even if it looks legitimate.
Never click on suspicious links; hover over them first to see the real URL.
If an offer sounds too good to be true, it probably is a scam.
Legitimate organizations, banks, or government bodies will never ask for your password or OTP over the phone or email.
Use strong, unique passwords for all your online accounts and enable two-factor authentication.
Report any suspicious activity immediately to the concerned platform or cyber authorities.
Educate your family and friends about common scams to protect them too.

caseStudies.title: The 'Scholarship' Trap
caseStudies.story: Many Indian students have been targeted by fake scholarship offers. These scams often ask for a 'processing fee' or bank details to 'transfer the scholarship funds,' but no scholarship ever materializes, and the students lose their money.
caseStudies.takeaway: Never pay money to receive a scholarship; legitimate scholarships do not ask for fees.

caseStudies.title: Nigerian Prince Email Scam
caseStudies.story: This classic scam involves an email claiming a large sum of money needs to be transferred out of a country, and the recipient is promised a share if they help by sending a smaller 'advance fee' first. Millions have lost money to variations of this fraud over decades.
caseStudies.takeaway: Be skeptical of unsolicited offers promising large sums of money for a small upfront payment.

lessons.practice: Identify three suspicious emails or messages you have received this week (or create a hypothetical one based on common scams) and list the red flags for each. Practice reporting them mentally.

quiz.q: What is phishing?
quiz.a: Phishing is a cyberattack where scammers try to trick you into revealing personal information like passwords or bank details by pretending to be a trustworthy entity, often through fake emails or websites.

quiz.q: Why should you never share your OTP (One Time Password)?
quiz.a: An OTP is a crucial security code that authorizes transactions or account access, and sharing it allows scammers to complete fraudulent activities using your account, like making payments or transferring money.

quiz.q: What is one simple way to check if a website link is safe before clicking?
quiz.a: You can hover your mouse cursor over the link (without clicking) to see the actual URL displayed, which often reveals if it's a legitimate site or a suspicious, misspelled address.

lessons.title: Screen time and digital wellbeing
lessons.why: Managing your screen time is vital for your health and happiness, just like eating well or exercising. Understanding digital wellbeing helps you use technology smartly, preventing eye strain, sleep problems, and even mental stress.

studyPlan.task: Read about how excessive screen time affects physical and mental health (eyes, sleep, posture).
studyPlan.read:
Excessive screen time is not just about tired eyes; it is a full-body experience that affects your physical and mental health. When you spend hours hunched over a smartphone or laptop, you are putting immense pressure on your neck and spine, often called 'Tech Neck.' This posture leads to chronic back pain and headaches. Mentally, the constant influx of information keeps your brain in a state of 'high alert,' which increases cortisol levels and can lead to anxiety or burnout over time.

Imagine an Indian student named Aryan who spends five hours daily on social media and gaming after his coaching classes. By 10 PM, he feels restless, his eyes are itchy, and he finds it hard to focus on his homework. This is because his brain is overstimulated and his eyes are suffering from Digital Eye Strain. The blue light from his phone tricks his brain into thinking it is still daytime, suppressing melatonin, the hormone that helps us sleep.

To manage this, start by recognizing the signals your body sends. If your neck feels stiff or your eyes feel dry, your body is asking for a break. A simple method to follow is the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds. This relaxes the eye muscles and prevents long-term strain. Additionally, ensure your screen is at eye level to keep your spine neutral and prevent posture-related pain.
checkpoints: What is 'Tech Neck' and how does it affect your physical health?
How does blue light impact your ability to fall asleep at night?
What are the three steps of the 20-20-20 rule for eye health?

studyPlan.task: Monitor your own screen time for a day using your phone's built-in tracker or an app.
studyPlan.read:
Most of us are unaware of how often we pick up our phones. Digital distractions are often subconscious habits triggered by boredom or a notification sound. To regain control, you must first face the data. Most modern smartphones have built-in trackers like 'Digital Wellbeing' on Android or 'Screen Time' on iOS. These tools show you exactly how many hours you spend on specific apps and how many times you unlock your phone in a day.

For example, a student might think they only use Instagram for ten minutes, but the tracker might reveal they actually spend two hours a day on it through multiple short sessions. This 'micro-scrolling' adds up quickly and fragments your focus, making it harder to engage in deep study. When you see that you have unlocked your phone 100 times in a day, it becomes clear that the device is controlling your attention rather than you using it as a tool.

Your task today is to open your settings and analyze your usage from the last 24 hours. Look at which apps take up the most time and at what time of day you are most active. Identify your 'top 3' time-consuming apps. Once identified, reflect on whether the time spent on these apps added any real value to your day or if it was just a way to kill time. Knowing your patterns is the first step toward changing them.
checkpoints: Which three apps currently consume most of your daily screen time?
How many times did you unlock your phone in the last 24 hours?
What is the difference between intentional use and micro-scrolling?

studyPlan.task: Research practical tips for reducing screen time and setting 'tech-free' zones or times.
studyPlan.read:
Setting boundaries is about creating physical and temporal space between you and your devices. Without rules, technology tends to bleed into every aspect of our lives, from the dinner table to the bedroom. Establishing 'Tech-Free Zones' helps your brain associate certain areas with relaxation and human connection rather than digital consumption. This reduces the urge to constantly check for updates.

Consider the common Indian household practice of having dinner together. If every family member is on their phone, the opportunity for meaningful conversation is lost. By setting a boundary like 'No phones at the dinner table,' you prioritize real-world interaction. Similarly, keeping your study desk free of smartphones ensures that your brain remains in a 'flow state,' allowing you to complete assignments faster and with better quality.

To implement this, start with two specific boundaries. First, create a 'Device Bedtime' where all screens are turned off at least 60 minutes before you sleep. Second, designate your dining area as a phone-free zone. If you find it hard to resist the urge, physically move your phone to another room or put it in a drawer. Out of sight truly becomes out of mind. Using 'Do Not Disturb' modes during study hours can also help maintain these boundaries by silencing non-essential pings.
checkpoints: Why is it beneficial to have tech-free zones in your home?
What is the recommended time to stop using screens before going to bed?
How does keeping a phone out of sight help with concentration?

studyPlan.task: Watch a TED Talk or read an article on the benefits of taking a break from digital devices.
studyPlan.read:
A digital detox is a designated period where you intentionally reduce or eliminate screen use to recharge your mental health. In a world of constant notifications, our brains are rarely at rest. Taking a break allows your dopamine levels to reset, leading to improved mood, better focus, and increased creativity. It is like hitting the refresh button on your brain's processing power.

Many successful students and professionals use digital detoxes to prevent burnout. You might find that without the distraction of Reels or YouTube shorts, you suddenly have time for old hobbies like playing cricket, reading a physical book, or painting. A short detox can prove that you don't actually 'need' to be online every minute to stay happy or informed. It breaks the cycle of FOMO, or the 'Fear Of Missing Out.'

You can start small with a 'Digital Sabbath'—perhaps four hours on a Sunday afternoon where you leave your phone in a cupboard and go for a walk or talk to your grandparents. During this time, observe your feelings. You might feel anxious at first, but that feeling usually transitions into a sense of calm and clarity. Notice how much more 'present' you feel in your physical surroundings when you aren't viewing the world through a camera lens or a social media feed.
checkpoints: What is the psychological benefit of a 'dopamine reset' during a detox?
What does FOMO stand for, and how does a detox help reduce it?
How can a short digital break improve your creativity or hobbies?

studyPlan.task: Learn about the impact of blue light on sleep and explore settings like 'night mode' on your devices.
studyPlan.read:
Your body has an internal clock called the circadian rhythm, which tells you when to wake up and when to sleep. Light is the primary signal that regulates this rhythm. Screens emit a high concentration of blue light, which mimic's the sun's rays. When you use a screen late at night, your brain thinks it is daytime and stops producing melatonin, the hormone required for deep, restorative sleep.

Poor sleep doesn't just make you tired; it affects your memory, your ability to learn new concepts, and your emotional stability. For an Indian student preparing for exams, losing even an hour of quality sleep due to late-night scrolling can significantly lower test performance. Deep sleep is when your brain 'archives' what you learned during the day, so protecting your sleep is actually a study strategy.

To fix this, explore your device settings for 'Night Mode,' 'Blue Light Filter,' or 'Eye Comfort Shield.' These settings shift the screen colors to a warmer, yellowish tone, which is less disruptive to your sleep cycle. Set these filters to turn on automatically at sunset. Better yet, switch to a physical book or a Kindle with e-ink if you must read before bed. Small changes in how you handle light at night can lead to massive improvements in your energy levels the next morning.
checkpoints: How does blue light affect the production of melatonin in the brain?
What is the function of 'Night Mode' on digital devices?
Why is deep sleep important for a student's memory and learning?

studyPlan.task: Practice mindful technology use by asking 'why am I picking up my phone?' before checking it.
studyPlan.read:
Mindfulness is the practice of being fully present in the moment. Mindful tech use means using your phone with a clear intention rather than out of mindless habit. Have you ever picked up your phone to check the weather and ended up scrolling through social media for thirty minutes? That is mindless use. It wastes time and leaves you feeling drained instead of refreshed.

Before you touch your phone, try the 'Wait and Ask' method. Pause for three seconds and ask yourself: Why am I picking up this device? Is it for a specific task, or am I just bored? Is there a better way to spend the next ten minutes? If you are picking it up just because you feel a slight discomfort or boredom, try sitting with that feeling for a minute instead of reaching for a digital escape.

Another technique is to 'clean' your digital environment. Turn off all non-human notifications. You need to know if your mother calls or a friend messages, but you don't need a buzz every time a random app wants to sell you something or someone likes an old photo. By minimizing these external triggers, you stay in the driver's seat of your attention. Practice being 'single-tasking'—if you are using an app for study, don't switch to another app until that task is complete.
checkpoints: What does it mean to use technology with 'clear intention'?
What is the 'Wait and Ask' method for reducing mindless scrolling?
Why should you turn off non-human notifications on your phone?

studyPlan.task: Develop a personal digital wellbeing plan for the next week, including specific goals for screen time and breaks.
studyPlan.read:
Today is about taking everything you have learned and turning it into a sustainable lifestyle. Digital wellbeing isn't a one-time fix; it is a continuous practice of balance. A personal plan helps you stay committed when the initial motivation wears off. It acts as a contract with yourself to protect your time, health, and focus while still enjoying the benefits of the digital world.

Your plan should be realistic. If you currently use your phone for six hours, trying to cut it to one hour immediately might fail. Instead, aim for gradual improvement. For example, an Indian student's plan might include: 'I will use a physical alarm clock instead of my phone to avoid morning scrolling,' and 'I will limit gaming to 45 minutes after my homework is finished.' These are specific, measurable goals that are easy to track.

Write down your plan and place it near your study area. Include your 'Tech-Free' zones, your blue light settings, and your daily screen time limit. Remember that technology is a powerful tool designed to help you connect and learn. By setting these rules, you are not losing out on anything; instead, you are gaining more time for your family, your health, and your future. Review your plan at the end of every week to see where you succeeded and where you can improve.
checkpoints: Why is it better to set gradual goals rather than extreme ones for screen time?
What are two specific goals you can include in your personal wellbeing plan?
How does a physical alarm clock help in reducing morning screen time?

notes: Excessive screen time can lead to eye strain, headaches, poor posture, and reduced physical activity.
Blue light emitted by screens can disrupt your sleep cycle, making it harder to fall asleep.
Constant digital stimulation can contribute to anxiety, stress, and difficulty concentrating.
Regularly taking short breaks (e.g., 20-20-20 rule for eyes) can mitigate physical discomfort.
Set clear boundaries for screen use, like 'no phones at the dinner table' or 'no screens an hour before bed'.
Use your device's built-in tools to monitor and manage your app usage and screen time.
Prioritize in-person interactions and outdoor activities over endless scrolling.
Remember that technology is a tool; learn to control it rather than letting it control you.

caseStudies.title: The 'Facebook Experiment' on Mood
caseStudies.story: A study published in the American Journal of Epidemiology in 2017 found that using Facebook extensively was associated with reduced well-being, including lower levels of happiness and life satisfaction.
caseStudies.takeaway: Mindless scrolling on social media can negatively impact your mental well-being; use platforms intentionally.

caseStudies.title: Teen Screen Time and Mental Health
caseStudies.story: Psychologist Jean Twenge's research, notably in her book 'iGen,' highlights a correlation between increased smartphone use among adolescents and a rise in mental health issues like depression and anxiety, emphasizing the importance of balancing digital and real-world interactions.
caseStudies.takeaway: Balance your screen time with offline activities to protect your mental health and foster real-world connections.

lessons.practice: Set a timer for 30 minutes. During this time, completely avoid checking your phone or any social media. Focus on a non-digital activity like reading a book, drawing, or talking to someone in person.

quiz.q: What is the 20-20-20 rule for eye strain?
quiz.a: For every 20 minutes spent looking at a screen, you should look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds to help reduce eye strain.

quiz.q: How does blue light from screens affect your sleep?
quiz.a: Blue light suppresses the production of melatonin, a hormone that helps you sleep, making it harder to fall asleep and disrupting your natural sleep cycle.

quiz.q: Name one benefit of a 'digital detox'.
quiz.a: A digital detox can improve focus, reduce stress and anxiety, enhance sleep quality, and encourage more real-world social interaction.

lessons.title: Copyright, plagiarism and fair use
lessons.why: Understanding copyright, plagiarism, and fair use is crucial for anyone creating or using content online. It teaches you to respect others' work, protect your own creations, and navigate the digital world ethically and legally, especially for school projects and future careers.

studyPlan.task: Read about what copyright is and what types of work it protects (e.g., books, music, art, software).
studyPlan.read:
Copyright is a legal right that gives the creator of an original work exclusive control over how it is used. In India, the Copyright Act of 1957 governs these rules. When you write a poem, record a song, or code a new app, you automatically own the copyright the moment your work is fixed in a tangible form. It protects literary works like your school essays, artistic works like your sketches, and even software code.

Think of copyright like a 'No Trespassing' sign for intellectual property. If you spend hours creating a digital painting and post it on Instagram, someone else cannot legally print it on t-shirts and sell them without your permission. This protection ensures that creators are rewarded for their hard work and creativity, encouraging more people to innovate.

To understand what copyright covers, remember these categories: Literary works including books and lyrics, Dramatic works like plays, Musical compositions, Artistic works like photographs and paintings, Cinematograph films, and Sound recordings. A simple method to check if something is copyrighted is to assume everything you find online belongs to someone else unless it explicitly says 'Public Domain'.

When you see the little 'c' in a circle symbol, it is a reminder of these rights. Even without that symbol, the law protects the creator. As a student, respecting these rights is the first step toward becoming a responsible digital citizen.
checkpoints: What are three types of creative work protected by copyright law?
Does a creator need to register their work to have basic copyright protection?
Why is copyright important for creators in India?

studyPlan.task: Learn about different forms of plagiarism and why it's considered unethical in academics and beyond.
studyPlan.read:
Plagiarism is the act of presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own, with or without their consent. In Indian schools and universities, this is a serious academic offense. It is not just about copying word-for-word; it also includes 'patchwriting,' where you change a few words in a sentence but keep the structure the same, or failing to acknowledge the source of a unique idea.

Imagine you are writing a history report on the Taj Mahal. You find a great paragraph on a travel blog and paste it directly into your assignment without quotation marks or a mention of the author. Even if you change 'beautiful' to 'stunning,' if the core thought isn't yours, it is plagiarism. This is unethical because it is essentially stealing intellectual credit and prevents you from actually learning the material.

To avoid this, follow the 'Quote and Credit' method. If you use a direct sentence, put it in quotation marks. If you summarize an idea in your own words, still mention where you read it. Always keep a list of websites and books you visit while researching so you don't forget where your information came from. Honesty in your work builds your reputation as a scholar and professional.
checkpoints: What is the difference between copying and paraphrasing without credit?
Is it still plagiarism if you change a few words in a copied sentence?
Why is plagiarism considered a serious ethical issue in education?

studyPlan.task: Explore the concept of 'fair use' and its four factors, focusing on how it applies in educational settings.
studyPlan.read:
Fair Use is a legal doctrine that allows you to use small parts of copyrighted material without asking for permission. This is what allows students to include a few lines of a poem in a school report or a movie critic to show a short clip in a review. However, Fair Use is not a 'free pass' to use whatever you want; it is a limited exception.

There are four factors used to decide if a use is 'fair.' First is the Purpose: is it for non-profit education or commercial profit? Second is the Nature of the work: using a factual news report is easier to justify than using a private creative diary. Third is the Amount: using one sentence from a book is likely fair, but using an entire chapter is not. Fourth is the Effect on the market: if your use stops people from buying the original work, it is likely not fair use.

For an Indian student, a common example is using a map from a textbook in a classroom presentation. Since the purpose is educational and it doesn't replace the need for other students to buy the textbook, it usually falls under fair use. To stay safe, always ask: Am I using only what is necessary? Does my work add something new, like a commentary or analysis?
checkpoints: What are the four factors used to determine Fair Use?
Does using a copyrighted image for a school project always count as Fair Use?
How does the 'Effect on the Market' factor influence copyright decisions?

studyPlan.task: Practice citing a few online sources (e.g., a Wikipedia article, a news report) using a standard citation style (e.g., MLA or APA basics).
studyPlan.read:
Citing your sources is the professional way to give credit to the people whose ideas you have borrowed. It acts as a roadmap for your readers, allowing them to find the original information if they want to learn more. While there are complex styles like APA or MLA, the core goal is to provide enough information to identify the source.

Suppose you are citing a news article from the 'Times of India' website. A basic citation should include the author's name, the title of the article, the name of the website, the date it was published, and the URL. For a Wikipedia article, since the authors are many, you would list the article title, the site name, and the date you accessed it, because Wikipedia pages change frequently.

Follow these three steps for every source: 1. Identify the creator and title. 2. Note the location, such as the website link or book publisher. 3. Format it clearly at the end of your document in a section titled 'References' or 'Works Cited.' By doing this, you protect yourself from accusations of plagiarism and show that you have done thorough research. It makes your work look more credible and authoritative to your teachers.
checkpoints: What are the key pieces of information needed to cite an online news article?
Why is it important to include the 'date of access' for web pages?
Where should you place your list of sources in a school report?

studyPlan.task: Discover Creative Commons licenses as an alternative to full copyright and how to find CC-licensed content.
studyPlan.read:
Creative Commons (CC) is a system that sits between 'All Rights Reserved' and 'Public Domain.' It allows creators to give the public permission to share and use their creative work under conditions of their choice. This is incredibly helpful for students looking for images or music for their projects without worrying about complex legal permissions.

There are different CC licenses. The 'BY' or 'Attribution' license is the most common; it means you can use the work as long as you give credit to the creator. Some licenses have a 'NC' or 'Non-Commercial' tag, meaning you can't use it to make money. Others have an 'ND' or 'No-Derivatives' tag, meaning you can use the work but you cannot change or edit it.

To find these materials, you can use the 'Usage Rights' filter on Google Images or search on sites like Wikimedia Commons and Pixabay. A simple method for using CC content is the TASL approach: Title of the work, Author's name, Source (link to the work), and License (which CC license it uses). This ensures you are legally safe and respectful to the generous creators who share their work freely.
checkpoints: What does the 'CC BY' license require you to do?
How does Creative Commons differ from traditional copyright?
What does the 'NC' symbol mean in a Creative Commons license?

studyPlan.task: Think about how you would want your original school projects or creative works to be protected online.
studyPlan.read:
As a student living in a digital age, you are not just a consumer; you are a creator. Every time you post a video on YouTube, write a blog post, or submit a digital project, you have rights over that content. Protecting your work means deciding how you want others to interact with it. Do you want full control, or are you happy for others to share it with credit?

If you create a unique science project video, you might want to protect it by adding a copyright notice or choosing a specific Creative Commons license. If you find someone has re-uploaded your video as their own, you have the right to report it for copyright infringement. In India, platforms like YouTube have clear systems to help you take down stolen content.

Steps to protect your work: First, always keep proof of creation, such as original project files or drafts. Second, clearly state your name and the year of creation on your work. Third, consider your privacy settings; sharing only with friends or teachers reduces the risk of your work being stolen by strangers. Understanding your own rights helps you value the rights of others.
checkpoints: When does copyright protection begin for a student's original project?
What can you do if you find your original work has been stolen online?
Why is it important to keep original drafts or files of your work?

studyPlan.task: Reflect on how to create content ethically, ensuring all borrowed elements are properly attributed or used within fair use guidelines.
studyPlan.read:
Ethical content creation is about more than just avoiding lawsuits; it is about contributing to a healthy and respectful digital community. When you create a video, a presentation, or a social media post, you should aim to be a 'Good Digital Citizen.' This means being honest about what is yours and what is borrowed.

An ethical creator follows a simple checklist. Ask yourself: Did I add my own unique perspective or just copy others? Did I give credit to every source I used? If I used a song or an image, did I check if I had the right to use it? For example, if you make a meme using a screenshot from a Bollywood movie, while it might be fair use for satire, it is still ethical to acknowledge the source if you are using it in a larger project.

By following these principles, you build a brand of integrity. In your future career, whether you become a journalist, an engineer, or an artist, your ethics will be your most valuable asset. People trust creators who are honest about their influences and who respect the hard work of their peers. Remember, the digital world is a shared space; treat others' intellectual property as you would want yours to be treated.
checkpoints: What does it mean to be an 'Ethical Creator'?
Why is integrity important for your future career in the digital world?
What is one question you should ask yourself before publishing borrowed content?

notes: Copyright protects original works of authorship like books, music, art, and software from unauthorized use.
Plagiarism is using someone else's words or ideas without giving them credit, presenting them as your own.
Always cite your sources, even when paraphrasing, to avoid plagiarism.
Fair Use allows limited use of copyrighted material without permission for purposes like education, criticism, and news reporting.
The four factors of Fair Use include purpose and character of use, nature of the copyrighted work, amount used, and effect on the market.
Creative Commons licenses offer creators a way to allow others to use their work under specific conditions.
Ignorance of copyright law is not an excuse for infringement.
When in doubt, always ask for permission or use public domain/royalty-free content.

caseStudies.title: George Harrison's 'My Sweet Lord' Plagiarism Case
caseStudies.story: The former Beatle George Harrison was found guilty of 'subconscious plagiarism' for his hit song 'My Sweet Lord,' which was ruled to have substantially copied The Chiffons' earlier song 'He's So Fine.'
caseStudies.takeaway: Even accidental or subconscious copying can lead to copyright infringement; always strive for originality.

caseStudies.title: Students Expelled for Plagiarism at Delhi University
caseStudies.story: Several reports highlight cases where students at top Indian universities like Delhi University have faced severe penalties, including expulsion, for plagiarizing academic papers and dissertations, underscoring the strict stance against academic dishonesty.
caseStudies.takeaway: Academic plagiarism has serious consequences, including suspension or expulsion from educational institutions.

lessons.practice: Find an image online that you want to use for a school project. Determine if it's copyrighted, under Creative Commons, or public domain. If copyrighted, explain how you would either ask for permission, use it under fair use (if applicable), or find an alternative royalty-free image.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between copyright and plagiarism?
quiz.a: Copyright is a legal right that protects creators' original works, while plagiarism is an ethical offense of using someone else's work without attribution, regardless of copyright status.

quiz.q: Can you use a small part of a copyrighted song in your school video project without permission?
quiz.a: Possibly, under 'fair use' for educational purposes, but it depends on factors like how much you use, its impact on the original work's market, and whether you transform it.

quiz.q: What does a 'Creative Commons Attribution' (CC BY) license mean?
quiz.a: It means you are free to use, share, and adapt the work, even commercially, as long as you give appropriate credit to the original creator.

lessons.title: Ethics of AI and technology
lessons.why: As AI and technology shape our future, understanding their ethical implications is paramount. It helps you think critically about privacy, bias, and control, preparing you to be a responsible user and even a creator in a world increasingly run by smart machines.

studyPlan.task: Read an introduction to the ethical dilemmas posed by Artificial Intelligence (e.g., job displacement, autonomous weapons).
studyPlan.read:
Artificial Intelligence is no longer a concept from science fiction; it is part of our daily lives in India, from UPI payment security to movie recommendations on streaming apps. AI ethics is the field of study that asks whether these systems are doing the right thing. It is not just about whether a machine works, but whether it is fair, safe, and beneficial to humanity. As we integrate AI into critical sectors like healthcare and defense, we face dilemmas. For instance, if an AI system decides who gets a bank loan, is it using fair criteria?

Consider an Indian student using an AI-based career counseling app. The AI might suggest engineering to a boy and teaching to a girl based on old patterns it found online. This is an ethical issue because the machine is reinforcing stereotypes rather than looking at individual potential. Ethics helps us set boundaries to ensure technology serves us without taking away our agency or dignity. It covers big questions like job loss due to automation and the scary possibility of autonomous weapons that can make life-or-death decisions without a human pulling the trigger.

To begin thinking ethically, follow these three steps: First, identify the stakeholders, or who is affected by the AI. Second, consider the potential harms, such as loss of privacy or unfair treatment. Third, ask if the outcome aligns with human values like honesty and kindness. By questioning technology instead of blindly accepting it, you become a conscious digital citizen rather than just a consumer.
checkpoints: What is the primary goal of AI ethics?
Why is human agency important when using AI systems?
Identify one major ethical dilemma mentioned in today's reading.

studyPlan.task: Explore how biases in training data can lead to unfair or discriminatory outcomes in AI systems (e.g., facial recognition).
studyPlan.read:
AI systems learn from data provided by humans. If that data contains prejudices, the AI will learn and amplify those biases. This is called Algorithmic Bias. It is dangerous because people often assume machines are objective and neutral, but a machine is only as fair as the data it is fed. If a database of 'successful employees' mostly contains men from one specific region, the AI will learn to favor those candidates and reject others, regardless of their actual skills.

In India, this is visible in facial recognition technology. Many global AI models are trained on Western faces. When these systems are used in India, they may struggle to accurately identify diverse Indian skin tones or traditional attire, leading to errors. Imagine a student being marked absent or denied entry to an exam hall because a biased AI camera failed to recognize their face. This isn't just a technical glitch; it is an ethical failure that leads to discrimination and exclusion.

To spot bias, you should use the Diversity Check method. When you see an AI output, ask: Who was included in the training data? Who might be excluded? Does this result favor one group over another? If you are ever building a project, ensure your dataset includes a wide variety of perspectives, ages, and backgrounds to minimize the risk of the machine 'learning' to be unfair.
checkpoints: How does human bias enter an AI system?
What is a real-world consequence of biased facial recognition?
What are the three questions in the Diversity Check method?

studyPlan.task: Understand the ethical concerns around how AI uses and protects personal data, and the concept of 'surveillance capitalism'.
studyPlan.read:
Every time you use a free app, you are likely trading your personal data for a service. AI thrives on this data to predict your behavior. This has led to a concept called 'Surveillance Capitalism,' where companies treat your private habits as a raw material to be sold or used for profit. The ethical concern here is that AI can infer very sensitive things about you, like your health status, political leanings, or even your current mood, even if you never explicitly shared that information.

For a student in India, this might mean that an educational app tracks how long you hover over a specific question. While this could help you learn, it could also be sold to advertisers who target you with expensive coaching classes when you are feeling most vulnerable or frustrated. The line between 'helpful personalization' and 'intrusive surveillance' is very thin. Once your data is in a system, it is hard to get back, and if that system is hacked, your digital identity is at risk.

To protect yourself, practice the Data Minimalism approach. First, check app permissions and disable access to your camera, location, or contacts unless absolutely necessary. Second, read the 'Privacy Policy' summaries to see if they sell data to third parties. Third, use privacy-focused tools like 'Incognito' modes or encrypted messaging. Remember, just because a service is free doesn't mean it doesn't have a cost to your privacy.
checkpoints: Define 'Surveillance Capitalism' in your own words.
How can AI infer sensitive information you haven't shared?
List two steps of the Data Minimalism approach.

studyPlan.task: Discuss who is responsible when an AI makes a harmful decision (e.g., self-driving car accident, medical diagnosis).
studyPlan.read:
When a human makes a mistake, we know who to hold responsible. But when an AI makes a harmful decision, the lines of accountability become blurry. This is often called the 'Black Box' problem because complex AI models make decisions in ways that even their creators cannot fully explain. If a self-driving car in a busy Indian city has an accident, who is at fault? Is it the software programmer, the car manufacturer, or the person sitting in the driver's seat?

This is particularly critical in high-stakes areas like medicine. If an AI diagnostic tool in a rural clinic misidentifies a tumor, the consequences are life-altering. We must decide if we can trust a machine to make final decisions or if a human must always stay 'in the loop.' Accountability means there must be a clear path to explain how a decision was made and a way to seek justice if that decision causes harm. Without transparency, we cannot have true accountability.

To evaluate accountability, use the Chain of Responsibility framework. When using an AI tool, ask: Is there a human overseeing this? Can the AI explain 'why' it gave this result? Is there a way to appeal the decision? Always remember that technology should be a tool used by humans, not a replacement for human judgment and responsibility. As a user, always cross-verify AI-generated information before acting on it.
checkpoints: What is the 'Black Box' problem in AI?
Why is human-in-the-loop important for medical AI?
Name three stakeholders who might be responsible for an AI error.

studyPlan.focus: The future of work and AI
studyPlan.task: Research different perspectives on how AI will impact jobs and societal structures.
studyPlan.read:
One of the most debated ethical topics is how AI will change the way we earn a living. Automation is already taking over repetitive tasks in factories and call centers. While some argue that AI will create new, more creative jobs, others worry about massive unemployment, especially for those who don't have access to high-tech education. For students in India, where the job market is highly competitive, this transition is a major concern.

Think about the local 'Kirana' store or a delivery partner. If drones and automated inventory systems become the norm, these livelihoods are threatened. However, AI also creates roles for 'AI trainers,' 'data ethicists,' and 'prompt engineers.' The ethical challenge for society is ensuring that the benefits of AI-driven wealth are shared fairly and that workers are given the resources to learn new skills. We must avoid a future where the digital divide creates a massive gap between the 'tech-savvy' and the rest of the population.

To prepare for this shift, focus on 'Human-Centric Skills.' These are skills that AI struggles to replicate: deep empathy, complex problem-solving, ethical reasoning, and creative storytelling. While you should learn to use AI tools, do not rely on them for everything. Cultivate the ability to think critically and adapt to new technologies. The goal is to work alongside AI, using it to handle the boring tasks so you can focus on the uniquely human ones.
checkpoints: What is the 'digital divide' in the context of AI and jobs?
Give an example of a job that might be displaced and a new job AI might create.
What are 'Human-Centric Skills' and why are they important?

studyPlan.task: Identify examples of AI being used for positive social impact and potential risks of its misuse (e.g., deepfakes).
studyPlan.read:
AI is a powerful tool that can be used for immense good or significant harm. On the positive side, AI is being used in India to predict monsoon patterns for farmers, detect pests in crops using smartphone photos, and translate educational content into local regional languages. These are examples of 'AI for Good,' where technology helps solve societal problems and empowers the underserved. It shows that when ethics are prioritized, AI can be a force for equality.

However, the same technology can be misused. Deepfakes—AI-generated videos or audio that look and sound real—are being used to spread misinformation or harass individuals. During school elections or local community events, a deepfake could be used to ruin someone's reputation instantly. Another risk is the use of AI for mass surveillance, where people are tracked without their consent. The ethical boundary depends on 'intent' and 'consent.' Using technology to deceive or control others is a violation of digital ethics.

To navigate this, use the Intent-Impact Analysis. Before using or sharing an AI tool, ask: What is the intent of the creator? What could be the unintended impact on others? Is this respecting the consent of the people involved? Being an ethical digital citizen means celebrating the helpful uses of AI while remaining vigilant and vocal against its misuse for deception or harm.
checkpoints: Provide one example of how AI can help an Indian farmer.
What is a 'deepfake' and why is it an ethical concern?
What two factors help define the ethical boundary of an AI application?

studyPlan.task: Write down 2-3 ethical principles you believe AI systems should always adhere to.
studyPlan.read:
Now that you have explored the various facets of AI ethics—from bias and privacy to accountability and the future of work—it is time to define your own stance. As a student and future professional, you will interact with AI daily. You might even build AI one day. Having a set of personal principles helps you make consistent, ethical decisions when faced with new and confusing technologies. Principles act as a compass for your digital life.

Think about what matters most to you. Is it fairness? If so, you might pledge never to use AI tools that are known to be biased. Is it transparency? Then you might commit to always disclosing when you have used AI to generate a school project. In India, a country with immense diversity, a key principle could be 'Inclusion,' ensuring that any technology you support works for people of all languages, religions, and economic backgrounds. Your principles should reflect the kind of world you want to live in.

To formulate your principles, follow these steps: First, reflect on the most important human value you want technology to protect. Second, write a 'Should' statement (e.g., 'AI should always be transparent about its identity'). Third, apply this to a real scenario to see if it works. For example, if you believe in 'Privacy,' your principle might be: 'I will not use apps that require more data than they need to function.' These principles will help you remain a responsible and ethical leader in the age of AI.
checkpoints: Why are personal principles important for a digital citizen?
What is one example of a principle related to 'Inclusion'?
How can you test if your ethical principle is practical?

notes: AI ethics addresses the moral implications and societal impact of artificial intelligence systems.
Algorithmic bias occurs when AI systems reflect human biases present in their training data, leading to unfair results.
Privacy concerns arise from AI's ability to collect, analyze, and infer sensitive information about individuals.
Accountability in AI is complex; determining who is responsible for AI's errors or harms is a key challenge.
AI's impact on employment, requiring new skills and potentially displacing certain jobs, is a major ethical consideration.
Transparency (explainability) in AI is crucial; understanding how AI makes decisions helps build trust and identify biases.
The development of autonomous weapons systems raises profound ethical questions about human control and responsibility.
Ethical AI design should prioritize human well-being, fairness, safety, and respect for individual rights.

caseStudies.title: Amazon's Biased AI Recruiting Tool
caseStudies.story: Amazon developed an AI tool to streamline recruiting, but in 2018, they scrapped it because it showed bias against women. The AI had learned to penalize résumés that included the word 'women's' (as in 'women's chess club') because it was trained on historical data from a male-dominated tech industry.
caseStudies.takeaway: AI systems are only as unbiased as the data they are trained on; careful design is essential to prevent discrimination.

caseStudies.title: Aadhaar System's Privacy Concerns
caseStudies.story: India's Aadhaar unique identification system, while aiming to streamline public services, has faced significant ethical debates regarding privacy, data security, and potential for surveillance, leading to court cases and public discussions about balancing utility with individual rights.
caseStudies.takeaway: Large-scale data collection by technology systems, even with good intentions, requires robust privacy safeguards and public oversight.

lessons.practice: Watch a short documentary or read an article about a real-world application of AI (e.g., facial recognition, medical AI). Identify at least two ethical concerns raised by this application and suggest a way to mitigate one of them.

quiz.q: What is algorithmic bias?
quiz.a: Algorithmic bias occurs when an AI system produces unfair or discriminatory outcomes because of prejudiced assumptions embedded in its design or training data.

quiz.q: Why is transparency important in AI systems?
quiz.a: Transparency, or explainability, helps users and developers understand how an AI makes decisions, allowing them to identify and correct errors, biases, and ensure accountability.

quiz.q: Name one ethical concern related to AI and jobs.
quiz.a: One major concern is the potential for widespread job displacement as AI automates tasks, requiring societies to adapt and retrain workforces for new roles.

lessons.title: Being a good digital citizen
lessons.why: Being a good digital citizen means you use technology responsibly, respectfully, and safely. It's about building a positive online presence, protecting yourself and others, and contributing constructively to the digital world, just like being a good citizen in your community.

studyPlan.task: Read about the core tenets of digital citizenship: respect, educate, protect.
studyPlan.read:
Digital citizenship is about how you conduct yourself in the vast virtual world, which is just as important as how you behave in your physical school or neighborhood. It is built on three pillars: Respect, Educate, and Protect. Respect means treating every user with dignity and honoring their privacy. Educate involves learning how to use digital tools effectively and sharing correct information. Protect is about securing your personal data and your physical health from the harms of excessive screen time.

Imagine a student named Aarav who joins a new online study group for the board exams. A good digital citizen like Aarav wouldn't just jump in and start spamming links. He would first read the group rules, introduce himself politely, and ensure that the resources he shares are helpful to his peers. He realizes that his actions affect the group's atmosphere and the learning experience of others.

To start your journey, follow the 'REP' method. Respect: Always ask yourself if your comment is kind. Educate: Verify a link before you send it to a WhatsApp group. Protect: Never share your OTP or home address with strangers online. By following these three steps, you ensure that the internet remains a safe and productive space for everyone, including yourself.
checkpoints: What are the three core pillars of digital citizenship?
How does your online behavior affect your real-world reputation?
Can you identify one way to protect your personal information today?

studyPlan.task: Learn about rules for respectful communication online, including proper language and tone.
studyPlan.read:
Netiquette, or network etiquette, is the set of professional and social rules for acceptable online communication. Just as you wouldn't shout at a teacher in a classroom, you shouldn't use all-caps in a formal email because it is perceived as shouting. Good netiquette involves using proper grammar, avoiding offensive slang, and being mindful of the tone of your messages, which can often be misunderstood without facial expressions.

Consider Ananya, who is emailing her college professor about an assignment. Instead of writing 'Hey, why haven't u checked my paper?', she uses a professional subject line and writes, 'Dear Professor, I am writing to kindly follow up on my assignment submission.' This respectful approach ensures she gets a helpful response rather than creating conflict. It shows she understands the context of her communication.

To practice good netiquette, use the 'THINK' method before hitting send. Ask yourself: Is it True? Is it Helpful? Is it Inspiring? Is it Necessary? Is it Kind? If your message doesn't meet these criteria, take a moment to rephrase it. Avoid using sarcasm in public forums as it can easily be misinterpreted, and always credit others when you share their creative work or ideas.
checkpoints: Why is tone important in text-based online communication?
What does writing in all capital letters signify in netiquette?
What does the THINK acronym stand for?

studyPlan.task: Understand what cyberbullying is, its impact, and how to respond if you witness or experience it.
studyPlan.read:
Cyberbullying is the use of digital platforms to harass, threaten, or humiliate someone. Unlike physical bullying, it can happen 24/7 and reach a huge audience instantly. It includes spreading rumors, posting embarrassing photos without consent, or creating fake profiles to mock someone. The impact on the victim's mental health can be severe, leading to anxiety, social withdrawal, and a drop in academic performance.

Suppose a student in your class, Rohan, is being teased in a WhatsApp group chat because of a mistake he made during a sports match. Even if you didn't start the teasing, staying silent or laughing at the jokes makes you a 'bystander.' An active digital citizen would either tell the group to stop or reach out to Rohan privately to offer support. Being an 'upstander' means taking a stand against negativity.

If you encounter cyberbullying, follow these three steps: Don't Retaliate, as responding with anger often escalates the situation. Save Evidence by taking screenshots of the abusive messages or posts. Report and Block the bully using the platform's built-in tools, and talk to a trusted adult, like a parent or a teacher, about what is happening.
checkpoints: What is the difference between being a bystander and an upstander?
Why is it important to save screenshots of cyberbullying?
Who are two trusted adults you could talk to if you see online harassment?

studyPlan.task: Review your privacy settings on social media and other online platforms to control who sees your information.
studyPlan.read:
Privacy management is the process of controlling how much of your personal life is visible to the digital world. Many apps and social media platforms are designed to collect as much data as possible, which can be used for targeted advertising or, in worse cases, by identity thieves. Your personal information, like your phone number, school name, and current location, is valuable and should be guarded closely.

Think about Priya, who loves posting photos of her daily life on Instagram. She realizes that her account is set to 'Public,' meaning anyone in the world can see where she eats and where she goes to school. By switching to a 'Private' account and auditing her followers list, she ensures that only people she actually knows can see her updates. This simple change significantly reduces her risk of being tracked by strangers.

To manage your privacy effectively, follow these steps: First, go to the settings menu of your most-used apps and select 'Privacy.' Second, disable location sharing for apps that don't need it. Third, check your 'Tagged' photos and adjust settings so you have to approve them before they appear on your profile. Regularly reviewing these settings helps you maintain a safe boundary between your private life and the public internet.
checkpoints: What are the risks of having a completely public social media profile?
Why should you disable location services for most of your apps?
How often should you audit your privacy settings and follower lists?

studyPlan.task: Practice identifying fake news or misinformation by checking sources and looking for bias.
studyPlan.read:
In the digital age, we are flooded with information, but not all of it is true. Fake news and misinformation are often designed to trigger strong emotions like anger or fear, making you want to share them immediately. Being a critical thinker means questioning the source, the motive, and the evidence behind a story before you believe it or pass it on to your family and friends.

For example, you might receive a forwarded message on WhatsApp claiming that a local school is closing tomorrow due to an emergency. Instead of immediately forwarding it to all your classmates, a critical thinker would check the school's official website or a trusted local news portal. You might find that the message was an old prank from three years ago that has started circulating again.

Use the 'Sift' technique to verify information: Stop and check if the source is reliable. Investigate the creator's reputation. Find trusted coverage to see if other reputable news outlets are reporting the same thing. Trace the original context of photos or quotes, as they are often taken out of context to mislead people. Verifying facts takes an extra minute but prevents the spread of harmful lies.
checkpoints: What is the main goal of most fake news stories?
Why should you check multiple sources before sharing news?
What does it mean to trace a quote or photo back to its original context?

studyPlan.task: Reflect on your own online presence and consider what kind of digital footprint you want to leave behind.
studyPlan.read:
Your digital footprint is the permanent trail of data you leave behind whenever you use the internet. This includes your social media posts, comments on YouTube, and even the websites you visit. In the future, college admissions officers and employers in India and abroad often search for a candidate's online presence to understand their character. A negative footprint can close doors, while a positive one can create opportunities.

Imagine Ishaan, who is passionate about coding. Instead of just playing games online, he shares his small coding projects on LinkedIn and writes helpful comments on programming forums. When he applies for an internship, the recruiter sees his constructive contributions and passion. Ishaan's digital footprint works like a living resume that showcases his skills and his ability to interact professionally with others.

To manage your footprint, start by 'Googling' yourself to see what information is public. Delete old accounts you no longer use and remove any posts that don't reflect who you are today. Moving forward, think of the 'Grandmother Rule': if you wouldn't want your grandmother or a future employer to see it, don't post it. Focus on sharing content that shows your interests, your kindness, and your growth.
checkpoints: Who might look at your digital footprint in the future?
What is the 'Grandmother Rule' in the context of posting online?
How can a positive digital footprint help your career or education?

studyPlan.task: Identify one action you can take this week to contribute positively to an online community or support a friend online.
studyPlan.read:
The final step in being a great digital citizen is moving beyond just being 'safe' to being 'positive.' The internet can sometimes feel like a place of conflict, but you have the power to change that by being an active force for good. Promoting positivity means supporting others, sharing encouraging words, and using your digital skills to help your community or solve problems.

Consider a student named Meera who notices a friend is feeling down after receiving a low grade. Instead of ignoring it, she sends a thoughtful voice note with some helpful study tips and words of encouragement. Or consider a student who uses their social media to raise awareness about a local environmental issue. These small acts of kindness and activism turn the internet into a community rather than just a network of computers.

This week, choose one specific action to promote positivity. You could post a genuine compliment on a friend’s creative work, share a link to a verified charity, or help a younger sibling set up their privacy settings. By choosing to be helpful rather than hurtful, you contribute to a digital culture that values empathy and collaboration. Remember, digital citizenship is not just a set of rules; it is a commitment to being a good human being online.
checkpoints: How does supporting a friend online contribute to better digital citizenship?
What is one way you can use social media for a social cause?
Why is empathy important in digital interactions?

notes: A good digital citizen is respectful, responsible, and safe in their online interactions.
Think before you post; once something is online, it's very difficult to remove.
Respect others' opinions and privacy, even if you disagree with them.
Never engage in cyberbullying; if you see it, report it and support the victim.
Use strong, unique passwords and enable two-factor authentication to protect your accounts.
Be critical of information you find online; verify facts from reputable sources before believing or sharing.
Manage your digital footprint by being mindful of what you share and your privacy settings.
Promote a positive and inclusive online environment by being kind and helpful to others.

caseStudies.title: The Dangers of Online Shaming (Monica Lewinsky)
caseStudies.story: Monica Lewinsky became a global target of online shaming and cyberbullying during the late 1990s. Her experience highlights the severe psychological impact of widespread public ridicule and serves as a powerful reminder about empathy and the need for respectful online discourse.
caseStudies.takeaway: Consider the human impact of your words online; online shaming can cause severe and lasting harm.

caseStudies.title: Sanjana's Fake News Fight
caseStudies.story: Sanjana, a high school student in Mumbai, noticed her family WhatsApp group sharing misleading health remedies. She took the initiative to research reliable sources and politely shared factual information, helping her family members become more critical of forwarded messages.
caseStudies.takeaway: Be a fact-checker and respectfully counter misinformation to protect your community.

lessons.practice: Take one minute to critically evaluate a news headline or social media post you see online today. Ask yourself: Is this source credible? Is there any bias? Does it make me feel a strong emotion? Why?

quiz.q: What is 'netiquette'?
quiz.a: Netiquette refers to the rules of polite and respectful behavior when communicating or interacting with others online, similar to etiquette in the real world.

quiz.q: Why is it important to think before you post something online?
quiz.a: Once something is posted online, it can be permanent, widely shared, and difficult to control, potentially impacting your reputation and future opportunities.

quiz.q: What does 'digital footprint' mean?
quiz.a: Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave behind from your online activities, including websites visited, emails sent, and social media posts, which can be permanent and accessible.
